question: Classify glomerulonephritis. Describe the pathology of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
answer_html:
Definition Glomerulonephritis (GN) is inflammation of the glomeruli, usually caused by immune mechanisms (immune-complex deposition or antibodies against the glomerular basement membrane). It presents with blood and protein in the urine and may lead to kidney failure.

1. Classification A. By cause

  • Primary GN – disease starts in the kidney (e.g. minimal change disease, IgA nephropathy, membranous nephropathy).
  • Secondary GN – part of a systemic disease (post-infectious, SLE, diabetes, vasculitis, hepatitis B/C, HIV).

B. By clinical syndrome | Syndrome | Main features | Examples | |---|---|---| | Acute nephritic syndrome | Haematuria, oliguria, hypertension, oedema, mild proteinuria | Post-streptococcal GN, IgA nephropathy | | Nephrotic syndrome | Heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day in adults), hypoalbuminaemia, generalised oedema, hyperlipidaemia | Minimal change disease (children), membranous nephropathy, FSGS (adults) | | Rapidly progressive GN | Loss of kidney function in weeks; crescents in glomeruli | Goodpasture syndrome, vasculitis | | Chronic GN | Slowly progressive scarring → chronic kidney disease | End result of many GNs | | Asymptomatic haematuria/proteinuria | Detected on routine urine test | IgA nephropathy |

2. Acute post-streptococcal GN (APSGN) a) Aetiology and pathogenesis

  • Follows infection with nephritogenic strains of group A β-haemolytic streptococci – sore throat (1–3 weeks before) or skin infection/impetigo (3–6 weeks before).
  • Antigen–antibody complexes form and deposit in glomeruli (type III hypersensitivity) → complement activation → neutrophil infiltration and inflammation.
  • Most common in children aged 5–12 years, especially in crowded, low-hygiene settings.

b) Morphology

  • Gross: kidneys slightly enlarged, pale, with tiny petechial haemorrhages on the surface ("flea-bitten kidney").
  • Light microscopy: diffuse proliferative GN – glomeruli are enlarged and hypercellular due to proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells and infiltration by neutrophils; capillary lumens are narrowed.
  • Immunofluorescence: granular ("lumpy-bumpy") deposits of IgG and C3.
  • Electron microscopy: subepithelial electron-dense "humps".

c) Clinical features and investigations

  • Sudden puffiness of the face (periorbital oedema), smoky or cola-coloured urine, oliguria, hypertension, headache.
  • Urine: RBCs and RBC casts, mild proteinuria.
  • Blood: raised ASO titre (after throat infection) or anti-DNase B (after skin infection), low serum C3, raised urea and creatinine.

d) Prognosis

  • More than 95% of children recover completely with supportive care; a few develop rapidly progressive GN or chronic disease; prognosis is less favourable in adults.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Daily weight, intake–output, BP monitoring, salt and fluid restriction during oliguria, and watching for hypertensive encephalopathy and heart failure.
  • Prevention: prompt treatment of streptococcal sore throat and skin infections, and hygiene.

Conclusion Glomerulonephritis may present as nephritic or nephrotic syndrome. APSGN is an immune-complex disease after streptococcal infection, showing diffuse proliferative changes with subepithelial humps, and usually has an excellent outcome in children.

question: Describe the pathology of acute and chronic pyelonephritis.
answer_html:
Definition Pyelonephritis is inflammation of the kidney tubules, interstitium and renal pelvis, usually due to bacterial infection. It may be acute (suppurative) or chronic (with scarring).

A. Acute pyelonephritis 1. Aetiology and routes

  • Organisms: Escherichia coli (most common), Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas, Enterococcus.
  • Ascending infection (most common) – bacteria from the urethra and bladder reach the kidney, helped by vesicoureteric reflux (VUR).
  • Haematogenous spread – in septicaemia (Staphylococci).

2. Predisposing factors

  • Urinary obstruction (stones, BPH, strictures), VUR, catheterisation and instrumentation, pregnancy, diabetes mellitus, female sex, immunosuppression.

3. Morphology

  • Gross: kidney enlarged; yellow-white abscesses on the surface and cut section; congested pelvis.
  • Microscopy: patchy suppurative inflammation of the interstitium, neutrophils within tubules, neutrophil (WBC) casts, tubular destruction; glomeruli usually spared.
  • Complications: papillary necrosis (especially in diabetes and obstruction), pyonephrosis (pus filling the pelvis), perinephric abscess, septicaemia.

4. Clinical features

  • Sudden fever with chills, flank (loin) pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, dysuria, frequency, vomiting; urine shows pus cells, bacteria and WBC casts.

B. Chronic pyelonephritis 1. Types

  • Reflux nephropathy – due to VUR with infection from childhood (most common type).
  • Chronic obstructive pyelonephritis – recurrent infections above an obstruction.

2. Morphology

  • Gross: kidneys small and irregularly scarred; coarse, U-shaped corticomedullary scars, especially at the poles, overlying blunted and deformed calyces; may be unilateral or asymmetrical.
  • Microscopy: interstitial fibrosis, chronic inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, plasma cells), tubular atrophy; dilated tubules filled with pink colloid casts resembling thyroid follicles ("thyroidisation"); periglomerular fibrosis.

3. Effects

  • Hypertension, polyuria and nocturia (tubular damage), proteinuria, gradual chronic kidney disease.

C. Investigations that support the pathological diagnosis

  • Urine microscopy – plenty of pus cells, bacteria and WBC casts (WBC casts show that inflammation is in the kidney, not only in the bladder).
  • Urine culture – usually more than 10⁵ colonies/mL of a single organism; blood culture in septic patients.
  • Blood – raised total leucocyte count, CRP; creatinine may rise in severe or bilateral disease.
  • Ultrasound/CT – to look for obstruction, abscess or stones; micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) and DMSA scan in children to detect reflux and scars.
  • Chronic pyelonephritis – small irregular kidneys on imaging, proteinuria, rising creatinine.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Encourage fluids, timely and complete antibiotic courses, and relief of obstruction; collect urine culture before antibiotics; aseptic catheter care.
  • Children with recurrent UTI need evaluation for VUR to prevent kidney scarring.

Conclusion Acute pyelonephritis is a suppurative bacterial infection with interstitial abscesses and WBC casts, while chronic pyelonephritis shows coarse scars over deformed calyces with interstitial fibrosis and thyroidisation, leading to hypertension and kidney failure.

question: Describe the clinico-pathological features of renal calculi.
answer_html:
Definition Renal calculi (kidney stones, urolithiasis) are hard crystalline masses formed in the urinary tract from substances normally dissolved in urine. They are common in hot, dry regions – India's northern and western states form part of a recognised "stone belt".

1. Types of calculi | Type | Frequency | Features | |---|---|---| | Calcium oxalate / calcium phosphate | Most common (about 75–80%) | Hard, radio-opaque; linked to hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, low citrate, hyperparathyroidism | | Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate, "triple phosphate") | 10–15% | Form in alkaline urine with urease-producing bacteria (Proteus); can fill the pelvis and calyces as large staghorn calculi | | Uric acid | 5–10% | In acidic urine, gout, high cell turnover (leukaemia, chemotherapy); radiolucent on X-ray | | Cystine | 1–2% | Inherited cystinuria; hexagonal crystals; begin in childhood |

2. Pathogenesis

  • Supersaturation of urine with stone-forming salts due to low urine volume or high excretion.
  • Nucleation of crystals, followed by growth and aggregation.
  • Changes in urine pH (acidic – uric acid; alkaline – struvite, calcium phosphate).
  • Deficiency of inhibitors (citrate, magnesium) and presence of a nidus (debris, bacteria, foreign body).

3. Risk factors

  • Dehydration – hot climate, outdoor work, low water intake.
  • Diet high in salt, animal protein and oxalate; obesity, diabetes.
  • Hyperparathyroidism, prolonged immobilisation, recurrent UTI, gout, inflammatory bowel disease, family history, anatomical abnormalities.

4. Morphology

  • Usually unilateral, located in the calyces, pelvis or ureter; vary from sand-like particles to large staghorn stones.
  • Surrounding tissue shows chronic inflammation, fibrosis and sometimes squamous metaplasia of the pelvic lining.

5. Clinical features

  • Renal colic – severe, colicky loin pain radiating to the groin, with nausea and vomiting, when a stone moves into the ureter.
  • Haematuria, dysuria, frequency; sometimes passage of gravel.
  • Many stones are silent and found incidentally.

6. Complications

  • Obstruction → hydronephrosis, loss of kidney function.
  • Infection → pyelonephritis, pyonephrosis, urosepsis.
  • Rarely, squamous cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis with long-standing stones.

7. Investigations

  • Urine – RBCs, crystals, pH, culture; non-contrast CT KUB (most sensitive), X-ray KUB, ultrasound; serum calcium, uric acid, creatinine; analysis of passed stones to guide prevention.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Encourage 2.5–3 litres of fluid daily, strain urine to collect stones, give analgesics and monitor for fever (infected obstructed kidney is an emergency).
  • Teach dietary advice according to stone type.

Conclusion Renal calculi are mostly calcium oxalate stones formed by supersaturation of concentrated urine. They cause colic, haematuria, obstruction and infection; adequate hydration and treatment of risk factors prevent recurrence.

question: Describe the pathology of acute and chronic renal failure.
answer_html:
Introduction Renal failure is the inability of the kidneys to excrete waste products, regulate water, electrolytes and acid–base balance and perform hormonal functions. Acute renal failure (acute kidney injury, AKI) develops over hours to days and is often reversible; chronic renal failure (chronic kidney disease, CKD) develops over months to years and is progressive.

A. Acute renal failure (AKI) 1. Causes

  • Pre-renal (reduced blood flow) – dehydration, haemorrhage, shock, heart failure.
  • Renal (intrinsic) – acute tubular necrosis (ATN) (most common), acute glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis.
  • Post-renal – obstruction by stones, BPH, tumours.

2. Pathology of acute tubular necrosis

  • Ischaemic ATN (shock, sepsis, surgery) – patchy necrosis of tubular cells along the nephron, with rupture of basement membrane (tubulorrhexis).
  • Nephrotoxic ATN (aminoglycosides, contrast, heavy metals, snake venom, myoglobin, haemoglobin) – necrosis mainly of proximal tubules, basement membrane intact.
  • Gross: kidneys swollen, pale cortex, congested medulla.
  • Microscopy: loss of brush border, flattened or necrotic tubular cells, granular "muddy brown" casts blocking tubules, interstitial oedema; regenerating cells during recovery.

3. Clinical phases

  1. Initiation phase – the insult; urine output begins to fall.
  2. Oliguric (maintenance) phase – urine less than 400 mL/day; rising urea and creatinine, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, fluid overload.
  3. Diuretic phase – large urine volumes; risk of dehydration and hypokalaemia.
  4. Recovery phase – gradual return of function.

B. Chronic renal failure (CKD) 1. Causes (commonest in India)

  • Diabetic nephropathy, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, chronic glomerulonephritis, chronic pyelonephritis and obstruction, polycystic kidney disease; CKD of unknown aetiology in some farming communities.

2. Morphology ("end-stage kidney")

  • Gross: kidneys small, contracted, with finely granular surface (except in diabetes, amyloidosis and polycystic disease, where they may be normal-sized or large).
  • Microscopy: glomerulosclerosis (hyalinised glomeruli), interstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy, chronic inflammatory cells and thick-walled arterioles (arteriolosclerosis).

3. Effects of CKD (uraemic syndrome)

  • Anaemia (less erythropoietin), hypertension, fluid overload, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis.
  • Renal osteodystrophy (low vitamin D activation, high phosphate, secondary hyperparathyroidism).
  • Uraemic pericarditis, gastritis, neuropathy, itching, bleeding tendency.
  • Staging by eGFR: G1 ≥90, G2 60–89, G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 below 15 mL/min/1.73 m² (kidney failure).

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Strict intake–output, daily weight, potassium and creatinine monitoring in AKI; avoid nephrotoxic drugs.
  • CKD patients need BP and sugar control, diet modification, anaemia treatment and preparation for dialysis or transplant.

Conclusion Acute renal failure, usually due to tubular necrosis, causes rapid but often reversible loss of function with typical oliguric and diuretic phases. Chronic renal failure leads to small scarred kidneys with glomerulosclerosis and fibrosis and produces the multisystem features of uraemia.

question: Describe the pathology of renal cell carcinoma.
answer_html:
Definition Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common malignant tumour of the kidney in adults (about 85% of kidney cancers), arising from the tubular epithelium, mostly the proximal tubule. It is most common in men aged 50–70 years.

1. Risk factors

  • Smoking (most important modifiable factor), obesity, hypertension.
  • Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) syndrome and other inherited syndromes.
  • Acquired cystic disease of long-term dialysis patients; exposure to cadmium, asbestos, petroleum products.

2. Types | Type | Frequency | Genetics/features | |---|---|---| | Clear cell carcinoma | 70–80% | Loss of VHL gene on chromosome 3p | | Papillary carcinoma | 10–15% | Often multifocal, bilateral | | Chromophobe carcinoma | About 5% | Good prognosis | | Collecting duct carcinoma | Rare | Aggressive |

3. Morphology (clear cell type)

  • Gross: solitary, spherical mass, usually at the upper pole; golden-yellow cut surface (lipid) with areas of haemorrhage, necrosis and cysts ("variegated" appearance); tends to invade the renal vein, forming a tumour thrombus that may extend into the inferior vena cava.
  • Microscopy: sheets and nests of cells with abundant clear cytoplasm (glycogen and lipid dissolved during processing) and small nuclei, separated by a delicate vascular network.

4. Clinical features

  • Classic triad – haematuria, flank pain and palpable abdominal mass (present together in only about 10%).
  • Often detected incidentally on ultrasound/CT.
  • Fever, weight loss, left-sided varicocele (left renal vein block).
  • Paraneoplastic syndromes – polycythaemia (erythropoietin), hypercalcaemia (PTH-related peptide), hypertension (renin), Cushing syndrome – hence called the "internist's tumour".

5. Spread

  • Blood-borne spread is early – lungs ("cannon-ball" secondaries), bones, liver, brain; lymphatic spread to hilar and para-aortic nodes.

6. Prognosis

  • Depends on stage and grade; localised tumours are curable by nephrectomy; advanced disease is treated with targeted therapy and immunotherapy.

7. Staging and treatment in brief

  • Staging (TNM) depends on size, extension beyond the kidney capsule, renal vein or IVC involvement, nodes and distant metastases; renal vein invasion is common and worsens prognosis.
  • Radical or partial nephrectomy is the main treatment for localised tumours; RCC responds poorly to conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy, so advanced disease is treated with targeted drugs (tyrosine kinase inhibitors) and immunotherapy.
  • Five-year survival is high for small tumours confined to the kidney and low once distant spread has occurred.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Painless haematuria in an adult must always be investigated; nurses play a key role in smoking-cessation advice and post-nephrectomy care (monitoring urine output and the remaining kidney's function).

Conclusion Renal cell carcinoma, mostly of the clear cell type, is a golden-yellow tumour with clear cells that invades renal veins and spreads early by blood. Its varied presentation and paraneoplastic effects make early detection important.

question: Compare the pathology of benign prostatic hyperplasia and carcinoma of the prostate.
answer_html:
Introduction The prostate gland enlarges with age. Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and carcinoma of the prostate are both common in elderly men and both may cause urinary symptoms, but they differ in site, nature and outcome.

1. Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)

  • Definition: nodular hyperplasia of the glands and fibromuscular stroma of the prostate.
  • Cause: hormonal – dihydrotestosterone (DHT), formed by 5α-reductase, stimulates growth; increasing oestrogen–androgen ratio with age.
  • Age: begins after 40; present in most men above 70 years.
  • Site: transition zone and periurethral region (inner part of the gland) – compresses the urethra early.
  • Gross: enlarged, nodular gland; cut surface shows well-defined nodules, some solid, some with small cysts.
  • Microscopy: hyperplastic glands with two cell layers (inner columnar and outer basal cells), papillary infoldings, corpora amylacea, and proliferated smooth-muscle stroma.
  • Effects: lower urinary tract symptoms – frequency, nocturia, hesitancy, weak stream, dribbling, acute retention; bladder hypertrophy with trabeculation and diverticula, residual urine → UTI, stones, hydronephrosis.
  • Not premalignant.

2. Carcinoma of the prostate

  • Definition: malignant tumour, almost always adenocarcinoma, arising from prostatic glands.
  • Risk factors: old age, family history (BRCA2), race, diet rich in animal fat; androgen dependence.
  • Site: peripheral zone (posterior part) – so it can be felt as a hard, irregular nodule on digital rectal examination, and urinary symptoms appear late.
  • Gross: firm, grey-white or yellow ill-defined areas.
  • Microscopy: small, crowded glands lined by a single layer of cells (basal layer absent), enlarged nuclei with prominent nucleoli, invasion of stroma and perineural spaces.
  • Grading: Gleason score / Grade Groups based on gland pattern – guide prognosis and treatment.
  • Tumour marker: raised serum PSA (prostate-specific antigen).
  • Spread: local (seminal vesicles, bladder base), lymphatic (pelvic nodes), blood – bones, especially lumbar spine and pelvis, producing osteoblastic (bone-forming) secondaries with raised alkaline phosphatase; back pain may be the first symptom.

3. Comparison | Feature | BPH | Carcinoma prostate | |---|---|---| | Nature | Benign hyperplasia | Malignant (adenocarcinoma) | | Zone | Transition/periurethral | Peripheral (posterior) | | DRE | Smooth, firm, rubbery, enlarged | Hard, irregular, nodular | | Glands | Two cell layers | Single layer, no basal cells | | Urinary symptoms | Early | Late | | PSA | Normal or mildly raised | Often markedly raised | | Spread | None | Osteoblastic bone metastases |

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses care for men with retention (catheterisation), after TURP (bladder irrigation, watching for bleeding and TURP syndrome) and during hormone therapy; they also promote awareness of urinary symptoms and screening where advised.

Conclusion BPH is benign nodular hyperplasia of the inner prostate that causes early urinary obstruction, while carcinoma prostate is an adenocarcinoma of the peripheral zone that is detected by DRE and PSA and spreads to bones.

question: Describe the aetiology, pathogenesis and pathology of carcinoma of the cervix. Add a note on its screening.

diagram.caption: Progression from normal cervix to invasive carcinoma

invasive squamous cell carcinoma breaking the basement membrane; time scale of about 10–15 years

answer_html:
Introduction Carcinoma of the cervix is the second most common cancer among Indian women (after breast cancer) and a leading cause of cancer death in rural India. It is largely preventable because it develops slowly through detectable precancerous stages caused by human papillomavirus (HPV).

1. Aetiology and risk factors

  • Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types, especially HPV 16 and 18 (about 70% of cases) – the essential cause.
  • Cofactors: early age at marriage/first intercourse, multiple sexual partners (of the woman or her partner), high parity, smoking, HIV infection and immunosuppression, long-term oral contraceptive use, poor genital hygiene, low socio-economic status, lack of screening.

2. Pathogenesis

  1. HPV infects the immature basal cells of the transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction).
  2. Viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 inactivate the tumour-suppressor proteins p53 and Rb → uncontrolled cell division and accumulation of mutations.
  3. Precancerous changes – cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN):
    • CIN 1 (low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion) – lower one-third of epithelium; often regresses.
    • CIN 2–3 (high-grade lesion, including carcinoma in situ) – up to the full thickness.
  4. Breach of the basement membrane → invasive carcinoma; progression usually takes 10–15 years, giving a long window for screening.

3. Pathology

  • Types: squamous cell carcinoma (80–90%); adenocarcinoma (10–15%).
  • Gross: exophytic (cauliflower-like, friable, bleeds on touch), ulcerative, or endophytic (infiltrative, barrel-shaped cervix).
  • Microscopy: nests of malignant squamous cells with keratin pearls (well differentiated) or sheets of atypical cells (poorly differentiated), invading the stroma.

4. Spread

  • Direct – vagina, parametrium, bladder and rectum (fistulae); involvement of ureters causes hydronephrosis and uraemia (common cause of death).
  • Lymphatic – pelvic and para-aortic nodes; blood – late (lungs, liver, bones).

5. Clinical features

  • Post-coital bleeding, intermenstrual or post-menopausal bleeding, foul-smelling blood-stained discharge; later pelvic pain, urinary and bowel symptoms.

6. Screening and prevention

  • VIA (visual inspection with acetic acid) – precancerous areas turn white; recommended for women aged 30–65 years every 5 years under the national NCD screening programme; low cost, results immediate ("screen and treat" with cryotherapy or thermal ablation).
  • Pap smear (cytology) and HPV DNA testing; colposcopy and biopsy for positive cases.
  • HPV vaccination of girls aged 9–14 years (an indigenous quadrivalent vaccine, Cervavac, is available) – primary prevention.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses conduct VIA screening at health and wellness centres, motivate women to attend, explain results, and care for women undergoing radiotherapy and surgery.

Conclusion Carcinoma cervix results from persistent high-risk HPV infection progressing through CIN to invasive squamous cell carcinoma over many years. Screening by VIA/Pap/HPV tests and HPV vaccination can prevent most cases.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics

question: Classify ovarian tumours. Describe the gross and microscopic features of serous carcinoma of the ovary.
answer_html:
Introduction Ovarian tumours are common; most are benign, but ovarian cancer is often detected late and is a leading cause of death from gynaecological cancer. They are classified (WHO) according to the cell of origin.

(a) Classification of ovarian tumours (2 marks) 1. Surface epithelial tumours (65–70%; most ovarian cancers)

  • Serous – benign cystadenoma, borderline tumour, serous carcinoma.
  • Mucinous – cystadenoma, borderline, carcinoma (may be very large).
  • Endometrioid, clear cell (both associated with endometriosis), Brenner (transitional cell) tumour.

2. Germ cell tumours (15–20%; common in young women and girls)

  • Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) – most common benign tumour, containing skin, hair, teeth, sebaceous material.
  • Immature teratoma, dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumour (raised AFP), choriocarcinoma (raised hCG), embryonal carcinoma.

3. Sex cord–stromal tumours (5–10%)

  • Granulosa cell tumour (produces oestrogen → endometrial hyperplasia), thecoma, fibroma (with ascites and right pleural effusion = Meigs' syndrome), Sertoli–Leydig cell tumour (androgens – virilisation).

4. Metastatic tumours (about 5%)

  • Krukenberg tumour – bilateral ovarian secondaries with mucin-filled signet-ring cells, usually from the stomach; also from breast and colon.

(b) Serous carcinoma of the ovary (3 marks)

  • Most common malignant ovarian tumour; peak age 45–65 years; associated with BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations and family history; often bilateral.
  • Gross features:
    • Large tumour, partly cystic and partly solid, with papillary projections on the inner and outer surfaces.
    • Exophytic growth on the surface, adhesions; areas of haemorrhage and necrosis.
    • Serous (clear watery) fluid in cysts; frequently ascites and peritoneal deposits ("omental cake").
  • Microscopic features:
    • Complex branching papillae lined by stratified, markedly atypical cells with large hyperchromatic nuclei and many mitoses (high-grade serous carcinoma).
    • Destructive invasion of the stroma.
    • Psammoma bodies – concentric, laminated calcified bodies.
    • Low-grade serous carcinoma shows milder atypia.
  • Tumour marker: raised serum CA-125 (used for monitoring).
  • Spread: mainly by seeding over the peritoneum, omentum and diaphragm; lymphatic spread to pelvic and para-aortic nodes.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Vague symptoms (abdominal bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain) in older women should be investigated; nurses care for patients after debulking surgery and during chemotherapy and encourage genetic counselling for families with BRCA mutations.

Conclusion Ovarian tumours are classified into surface epithelial, germ cell, sex cord–stromal and metastatic types. Serous carcinoma, the commonest malignant type, is a cystic–solid papillary tumour with atypical stratified cells, psammoma bodies and early peritoneal spread.

question: Describe the pathology of gestational trophoblastic disease – hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinoma.
answer_html:
Introduction Gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) is a group of disorders arising from abnormal proliferation of placental trophoblast. All produce human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which is used for diagnosis and follow-up. The main forms are hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinoma.

A. Hydatidiform mole (vesicular mole) 1. Definition An abnormal pregnancy in which the chorionic villi become swollen, fluid-filled (hydropic) vesicles with trophoblastic proliferation.

2. Types | Feature | Complete mole | Partial mole | |---|---|---| | Karyotype | 46,XX (or 46,XY) – all chromosomes paternal (an "empty" ovum fertilised by one sperm that duplicates, or by two sperms) | Triploid (69,XXY) – normal ovum fertilised by two sperms | | Foetal parts | Absent | Present | | Villi | All villi swollen | Some villi swollen | | Trophoblast proliferation | Diffuse, marked | Focal, mild | | hCG | Very high | Moderately raised | | Risk of choriocarcinoma | About 2–3% (persistent disease 15–20%) | Very low |

3. Gross: uterus filled with grape-like clusters of thin-walled translucent vesicles ("bunch of grapes"). 4. Microscopy: large oedematous villi with central cavities (cisterns), absent or scanty blood vessels, proliferation of cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast. 5. Clinical features: bleeding in early pregnancy, uterus larger than dates, severe vomiting, early pre-eclampsia, passage of vesicles, very high β-hCG, "snowstorm" appearance on ultrasound, theca-lutein cysts, hyperthyroidism. 6. Management: suction evacuation; weekly serum β-hCG until normal for three consecutive weeks, then monthly for 6 months; reliable contraception (pills) during follow-up.

B. Choriocarcinoma 1. Definition: a highly malignant tumour of trophoblast without chorionic villi. 2. Antecedent pregnancy: about 50% after hydatidiform mole, 25% after abortion, about 22% after normal pregnancy, and some after ectopic pregnancy. 3. Gross: soft, haemorrhagic and necrotic mass in the uterine wall. 4. Microscopy: sheets of atypical cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast, extensive haemorrhage and necrosis, no villi. 5. Spread: early blood-borne spread – lungs (cannon-ball secondaries), vagina (bluish nodules), brain, liver, kidneys. 6. Features: persistent vaginal bleeding after a pregnancy, haemoptysis, raised hCG. 7. Prognosis: despite its aggressive nature, it is highly sensitive to chemotherapy (methotrexate, actinomycin D, combination regimens) with high cure rates.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses must stress regular hCG follow-up and contraception after molar evacuation, monitor for bleeding and pre-eclampsia, and give emotional support for pregnancy loss.

Conclusion Hydatidiform mole is an abnormal pregnancy with hydropic villi and trophoblastic proliferation (complete moles being paternal diploid), while choriocarcinoma is a villus-free malignant trophoblastic tumour that spreads early to the lungs but responds well to chemotherapy.

question: Describe the pathology of leiomyoma (fibroid) of the uterus.
answer_html:
Definition A leiomyoma (fibroid) is a benign tumour of the smooth muscle of the uterus (myometrium). It is the most common tumour in women, present in a large proportion of women of reproductive age.

1. Aetiology

  • Oestrogen- and progesterone-dependent growth – fibroids enlarge during pregnancy and shrink after menopause.
  • Risk factors: nulliparity, early menarche, obesity, family history, African ancestry; genetic changes (MED12 mutations) in tumour cells.

2. Location

  • Intramural (within the myometrium) – most common.
  • Submucosal (beneath the endometrium) – cause heavy bleeding and infertility; may become pedunculated and protrude through the cervix.
  • Subserosal (beneath the serosa) – may be pedunculated; may undergo torsion.
  • Cervical and broad-ligament fibroids are less common.

3. Gross features

  • Usually multiple, well-circumscribed, round, firm, grey-white masses with a false capsule (easily shelled out).
  • Cut surface shows a characteristic whorled (trabeculated) pattern.

4. Microscopic features

  • Interlacing bundles of uniform smooth-muscle cells with cigar-shaped nuclei.
  • No significant atypia, few mitoses, no necrosis.

5. Secondary (degenerative) changes

  • Hyaline degeneration (most common), cystic degeneration.
  • Red (carneous) degeneration – during pregnancy, due to haemorrhagic infarction; causes acute pain and fever.
  • Calcification – in postmenopausal women.
  • Fatty change, infection, sarcomatous change (leiomyosarcoma) – rare (less than 0.5%).

6. Clinical features

  • Many are asymptomatic.
  • Menorrhagia (heavy, prolonged periods) → iron-deficiency anaemia.
  • Pressure symptoms – frequency of urine, retention, constipation; abdominal mass.
  • Pain (degeneration, torsion), infertility and recurrent miscarriage, complications in pregnancy (malpresentation, PPH).

7. Diagnosis and treatment in brief

  • Bimanual pelvic examination – enlarged, firm, irregular uterus; ultrasound confirms number, size and site; haemoglobin for anaemia.
  • Medical treatment – iron, tranexamic acid and NSAIDs for heavy bleeding, hormonal treatment (progestins, LNG-IUS, GnRH analogues before surgery).
  • Surgery – myomectomy (removal of fibroids, preserving the uterus in women who wish to conceive) or hysterectomy (completed family, large or multiple fibroids); uterine artery embolisation in selected cases.
  • Rapid growth of a fibroid after menopause should raise suspicion of leiomyosarcoma, which shows marked atypia, many mitoses and tumour necrosis on microscopy.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses assess anaemia and bleeding, prepare women for myomectomy or hysterectomy, and explain that fibroids are benign and rarely become cancerous.

Conclusion Leiomyoma is a hormone-dependent benign smooth-muscle tumour with a firm, whorled cut surface. Its symptoms depend on its site and size, and degenerative changes such as red degeneration occur especially in pregnancy.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Special Pathology: Pathological Changes in Disease Conditions of Selected Systems
question: Describe the risk factors, types, pathology and spread of carcinoma of the breast.
answer_html:
Introduction Carcinoma of the breast is the most common cancer among women in India and worldwide. Indian women tend to develop it at a younger age and often present at an advanced stage, so awareness and early detection are vital.

1. Risk factors

  • Female sex and increasing age.
  • Family history and inherited mutations – BRCA1, BRCA2, TP53.
  • Prolonged oestrogen exposure – early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, first pregnancy after 30, not breastfeeding, hormone replacement therapy.
  • Obesity (after menopause), alcohol, sedentary life, radiation to the chest.
  • Previous breast cancer, atypical hyperplasia.

2. Types A. Non-invasive (in situ)

  • Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS).

B. Invasive

  • Invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type (70–80%).
  • Invasive lobular carcinoma (about 10%) – often bilateral and multifocal.
  • Special types – mucinous (colloid), medullary, tubular (better prognosis).
  • Inflammatory carcinoma – red, swollen breast; very aggressive.
  • Paget's disease of the nipple – eczema-like change of nipple with underlying carcinoma.

3. Pathology of invasive ductal carcinoma

  • Site: upper outer quadrant most commonly.
  • Gross: hard, grey-white, gritty mass with irregular, stellate (crab-like) margins; cuts with a grating sound ("unripe pear").
  • Tumour tethering to skin and ducts causes skin dimpling, nipple retraction; blocked lymphatics cause peau d'orange (orange-peel skin).
  • Microscopy: malignant cells in cords, nests and gland-like structures infiltrating a dense fibrous (desmoplastic) stroma.

4. Molecular (receptor) classification

  • Tested by immunohistochemistry: oestrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), HER2 and Ki-67.
  • Luminal A and B (ER-positive – respond to hormone therapy), HER2-enriched (respond to trastuzumab), triple-negative (ER, PR, HER2 negative – more common in young Indian women, aggressive).

5. Spread

  • Local – skin, chest wall.
  • Lymphatic – axillary lymph nodes (the most important prognostic factor), internal mammary and supraclavicular nodes.
  • Blood-borne – bones (spine, pelvis), lungs, liver, brain.

6. Early detection

  • Breast self-awareness/self-examination monthly, clinical breast examination (every 5 years for women aged 30–65 under the national NCD programme), mammography, followed by ultrasound and core biopsy of lumps.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses teach breast self-examination, perform clinical breast examination at screening centres, and care for patients after mastectomy (drain care, arm exercises, lymphoedema prevention, body-image support).

Conclusion Breast cancer is linked to genetic and hormonal factors and is most often an invasive ductal carcinoma – a hard, stellate mass in the upper outer quadrant that spreads first to axillary nodes. Receptor status guides treatment, and early detection greatly improves survival.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Special Pathology: Pathological Changes in Disease Conditions of Selected Systems
question: Describe the pathology of fibroadenoma and fibrocystic changes of the breast.
answer_html:
Introduction Most breast lumps in young women are benign. The two commonest benign conditions are fibroadenoma and fibrocystic changes. Distinguishing them from cancer relieves anxiety and avoids unnecessary surgery.

A. Fibroadenoma 1. Definition: a benign tumour of the breast containing both stromal (connective tissue) and epithelial (duct) elements – a biphasic tumour. 2. Age: young women, 15–30 years; may enlarge in pregnancy and regress after menopause (hormone-sensitive). 3. Clinical: a painless, firm, rubbery, well-defined, highly mobile lump – the "breast mouse"; usually single, sometimes multiple. 4. Gross: round or oval, well-circumscribed, encapsulated, grey-white, firm; cut surface is lobulated with slit-like spaces. 5. Microscopy:

  • Proliferation of loose fibroblastic stroma with ducts.
  • Intracanalicular pattern – stroma compresses ducts into slit-like spaces.
  • Pericanalicular pattern – stroma arranged around open, round ducts.
  • Duct lining shows normal two-layered epithelium. 6. Significance: simple fibroadenoma carries little or no increased cancer risk; it must be distinguished from phyllodes tumour (larger, faster growing, leaf-like pattern, cellular stroma, may recur).

B. Fibrocystic changes (fibrocystic disease) 1. Definition: the most common breast lesion, a group of changes due to exaggerated response of breast tissue to cyclical hormonal changes; seen in women aged 20–50 years. 2. Clinical: cyclical breast pain (mastalgia) and lumpiness, worse before periods; often bilateral, in the upper outer quadrants. 3. Gross: ill-defined areas of rubbery fibrosis with cysts of varying sizes; larger cysts contain brownish fluid and appear bluish ("blue-domed cysts"). 4. Microscopy:

  • Cyst formation with flattened or apocrine metaplastic lining (pink granular cells).
  • Fibrosis of stroma, adenosis (increased number of acini).

  • Epithelial hyperplasia in some cases. 5. Significance:

  • Non-proliferative changes (cysts, fibrosis, apocrine metaplasia) – no increased cancer risk.

  • Proliferative changes without atypia – slight increase in risk; atypical hyperplasia – significant increase in risk.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Every new lump needs triple assessment (clinical examination, imaging, needle biopsy/FNAC); nurses reassure women, teach breast awareness and advise supportive bras and pain relief for mastalgia.

Conclusion Fibroadenoma is a well-circumscribed, mobile biphasic tumour of young women, while fibrocystic change is a common hormone-related condition with cysts, fibrosis and apocrine metaplasia. Both are benign, but proliferative and atypical forms need follow-up.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Special Pathology: Pathological Changes in Disease Conditions of Selected Systems
question: Describe the pathology of stroke (cerebrovascular accident).
answer_html:
Definition Stroke (cerebrovascular accident) is a sudden focal (or global) neurological deficit lasting more than 24 hours or leading to death, due to vascular disease of the brain. It is a leading cause of death and disability in India.

1. Types | Type | Frequency | Main causes | |---|---|---| | Ischaemic stroke (cerebral infarction) | About 80–85% | Thrombosis on atherosclerotic plaques; embolism from the heart (atrial fibrillation, valve disease, MI) or carotid arteries; lacunar infarcts from small-vessel disease due to hypertension and diabetes | | Haemorrhagic stroke | About 15–20% | Intracerebral haemorrhage (hypertension – rupture of Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms; amyloid angiopathy in elderly); subarachnoid haemorrhage (rupture of berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis, AV malformation) |

2. Risk factors

  • Hypertension (most important), diabetes, smoking, dyslipidaemia, atrial fibrillation, heart disease, obesity, alcohol, previous TIA, old age, oral contraceptives in smokers.

3. Pathology of cerebral infarction

  • Brain infarcts undergo liquefactive necrosis.
  • First 12–24 hours: subtle changes; "red (eosinophilic) neurons", oedema.
  • 1–3 days: infiltration of neutrophils; softening of tissue.
  • 3 days to weeks: macrophages (gitter cells/foamy cells) remove necrotic debris.
  • Weeks to months: formation of a cystic cavity surrounded by gliosis (astrocytic scar).
  • Embolic infarcts are often haemorrhagic (red) because blood re-enters damaged vessels; thrombotic infarcts are usually pale (anaemic).
  • Lacunar infarcts – small (less than 1.5 cm) cavities in basal ganglia, internal capsule, pons.
  • Around the core lies the ischaemic penumbra – tissue that can be saved by early treatment (thrombolysis).

4. Pathology of intracerebral haemorrhage

  • Common sites – putamen and basal ganglia (most common), thalamus, pons, cerebellum.
  • Haematoma compresses and destroys tissue, causes raised intracranial pressure and may rupture into ventricles; later resolves into a cavity with brownish haemosiderin-stained walls.

5. Clinical correlation

  • Middle cerebral artery territory – contralateral hemiplegia (face and arm more than leg), sensory loss, aphasia (dominant hemisphere), neglect.
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage – sudden "worst ever" headache, neck stiffness, vomiting, loss of consciousness.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • "Time is brain" – nurses recognise stroke early (BE FAST: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time) and ensure urgent CT scan for thrombolysis decisions; prevention through BP control is a key community nursing task.

Conclusion Stroke is mostly ischaemic, due to thrombosis or embolism, producing liquefactive necrosis that ends in a cystic cavity with gliosis; haemorrhagic strokes result from hypertensive microaneurysms or berry aneurysms. Early recognition and risk-factor control reduce death and disability.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Special Pathology: Pathological Changes in Disease Conditions of Selected Systems
question: Write a note on tumours of the central nervous system.
answer_html:
Introduction Tumours of the central nervous system (CNS) arise from the brain, spinal cord and their coverings. They differ from tumours elsewhere because even benign tumours can be fatal when they press on vital areas within the rigid skull, and malignant brain tumours rarely spread outside the CNS.

1. Classification (simplified, WHO) | Group | Examples | |---|---| | Gliomas (from glial cells) | Astrocytoma (grades 1–4), glioblastoma (grade 4, most common primary malignant brain tumour in adults), oligodendroglioma, ependymoma | | Embryonal tumours | Medulloblastoma (cerebellum in children) | | Meningeal tumours | Meningioma | | Nerve-sheath tumours | Schwannoma (e.g. acoustic neuroma of the 8th cranial nerve), neurofibroma | | Sellar region tumours | Pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma | | Lymphomas and germ-cell tumours | Primary CNS lymphoma (in HIV), germinoma | | Metastatic tumours | Most common brain tumours overall – from lung, breast, melanoma, kidney, colon | Modern WHO classification also uses molecular markers (e.g. IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion).

2. Important tumours

  • Glioblastoma: adults above 50; cerebral hemispheres; variegated cut surface with haemorrhage and necrosis; microscopy – highly pleomorphic cells, pseudopalisading necrosis and vascular proliferation; very poor prognosis.
  • Meningioma: benign, middle-aged women; attached to the dura (extra-axial), compresses the brain; microscopy – whorls of meningothelial cells and psammoma bodies; usually curable by surgery.
  • Medulloblastoma: malignant tumour of the cerebellum in children; small round blue cells; spreads through CSF; radiosensitive.
  • Pilocytic astrocytoma: benign cystic cerebellar tumour of children – good prognosis.
  • Pituitary adenoma: hormonal effects (prolactinoma, acromegaly, Cushing) and bitemporal hemianopia from pressure on the optic chiasma.

3. Clinical features

  • Raised intracranial pressure – headache (worse in the morning), vomiting, papilloedema, drowsiness.
  • Seizures, focal deficits (weakness, speech, vision), personality change, endocrine disturbance.
  • In children, posterior fossa tumours cause ataxia and hydrocephalus.

4. Diagnosis and treatment in brief

  • CT and MRI with contrast show the site, size, oedema and mass effect; biopsy or excision gives the histological and molecular diagnosis.
  • Surgery (maximal safe removal), radiotherapy and chemotherapy (temozolomide for gliomas); dexamethasone reduces surrounding brain oedema; antiepileptic drugs control seizures.
  • Special features of CNS tumours: location matters more than histology; malignant tumours spread within the brain and through CSF but rarely outside the nervous system; the blood–brain barrier limits many drugs.
  • Prognosis ranges from excellent (meningioma, pilocytic astrocytoma) to very poor (glioblastoma, with survival usually measured in months).

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Neurological observations (GCS, pupils), seizure precautions, care before and after craniotomy, steroid therapy for brain oedema, and support to families are key nursing roles.

Conclusion CNS tumours include gliomas, meningiomas, embryonal tumours, nerve-sheath and pituitary tumours, with metastases being the commonest overall. Their effects depend more on location and raised intracranial pressure than on benign or malignant nature.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Special Pathology: Pathological Changes in Disease Conditions of Selected Systems
question: Define glomerulonephritis.
answer_html:
Glomerulonephritis (GN) is an inflammatory disease of the glomeruli of the kidney, usually of immunological origin (deposition of immune complexes or anti-glomerular antibodies), which results in haematuria, proteinuria, reduced glomerular filtration, oedema and hypertension.

  • Primary GN – disease limited to the kidney (e.g. IgA nephropathy, minimal change disease).
  • Secondary GN – part of systemic disease (post-streptococcal infection, SLE, diabetes, vasculitis).
  • Clinical forms – acute nephritic syndrome, nephrotic syndrome, rapidly progressive GN and chronic GN.
  • Commonest example in children: acute post-streptococcal GN – cola-coloured urine, periorbital puffiness and hypertension after a sore throat or skin infection.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Special Pathology: Pathological Changes in Disease Conditions of Selected Systems
question: Write the pathogenesis of carcinoma of the cervix.
answer_html:
Pathogenesis of carcinoma cervix

  1. Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV 16, 18) of the immature cells at the transformation zone of the cervix.
  2. Viral oncoproteins E6 (inactivates p53) and E7 (inactivates Rb) remove the brakes on cell division and DNA repair.
  3. Cofactors – smoking, HIV/immunosuppression, multiparity, early sexual activity – favour persistence and progression.
  4. Gradual progression through cervical intraepithelial neoplasia – CIN 1 → CIN 2 → CIN 3 (carcinoma in situ).
  5. Breach of basement membrane → invasive squamous cell carcinoma, usually over 10–15 years – allowing detection by VIA/Pap/HPV screening.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Special Pathology: Pathological Changes in Disease Conditions of Selected Systems
question: What is a hydatidiform mole?
answer_html:
A hydatidiform (vesicular) mole is an abnormal pregnancy of placental origin in which the chorionic villi become swollen and fluid-filled (grape-like vesicles) with proliferation of trophoblast; it belongs to gestational trophoblastic disease.

  • Complete mole – 46,XX of paternal origin, no foetus, all villi hydropic, very high hCG, 2–3% risk of choriocarcinoma.
  • Partial mole – triploid (69,XXY), foetal parts present, focal changes.
  • Features: bleeding in early pregnancy, uterus larger than dates, hyperemesis, very high β-hCG, "snowstorm" ultrasound.
  • Treatment: suction evacuation and serial β-hCG follow-up with contraception.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Special Pathology: Pathological Changes in Disease Conditions of Selected Systems
question: What is cryptorchidism? Mention its complications.
answer_html:
Cryptorchidism (undescended testis) is the failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum; the testis may lie in the abdomen, inguinal canal (most common) or high in the scrotal neck. It occurs in about 3% of full-term and up to 30% of preterm male babies; many descend spontaneously in the first 3–6 months.

Complications

  1. Testicular atrophy and infertility – higher temperature damages spermatogenesis.
  2. Increased risk of testicular germ-cell tumour (seminoma) – several times higher.
  3. Torsion and injury of the testis; associated inguinal hernia.
  4. Psychological distress.

Treatment: orchidopexy ideally between 6 and 18 months of age.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Special Pathology: Pathological Changes in Disease Conditions of Selected Systems
question: List the risk factors for carcinoma of the endometrium.
answer_html:
Carcinoma of the endometrium occurs mostly in post-menopausal women; most risk factors involve prolonged unopposed oestrogen stimulation.

  1. Obesity (oestrogen produced in fat), diabetes and hypertension.
  2. Nulliparity, early menarche and late menopause.
  3. Anovulatory states – polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
  4. Oestrogen-only hormone therapy without progestin; tamoxifen therapy.
  5. Oestrogen-secreting tumours (granulosa cell tumour); endometrial hyperplasia with atypia.
  6. Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer) and family history.

The typical early symptom is post-menopausal bleeding, which must always be investigated.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Special Pathology: Pathological Changes in Disease Conditions of Selected Systems
question: Define encephalitis and list its common causes.
answer_html:
Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain parenchyma, most often due to viral infection, presenting with fever, headache, altered consciousness, seizures and focal neurological signs. In India, such cases are reported under acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) surveillance.

Common causes

  1. Japanese encephalitis virus (Culex mosquito; pigs and birds are amplifying hosts) – preventable by JE vaccine.
  2. Herpes simplex virus (temporal lobes; treated with acyclovir).
  3. Dengue, measles, rabies, Nipah and Chandipura virus (sand-fly borne; first isolated from Chandipura village near Nagpur, Maharashtra).
  4. Bacterial, parasitic (cerebral malaria) and autoimmune causes.

Pathology: perivascular lymphocytic cuffing, microglial nodules and destruction of neurons (neuronophagia).

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Special Pathology: Pathological Changes in Disease Conditions of Selected Systems
question: Mention the risk factors for carcinoma of the penis.
answer_html:
Carcinoma of the penis is usually a squamous cell carcinoma of the glans or prepuce, seen in older men and more common in India than in Western countries.

Risk factors

  1. Phimosis and lack of circumcision – accumulation of smegma and chronic irritation.
  2. Poor genital hygiene.
  3. Human papillomavirus (HPV 16, 18) infection.
  4. Smoking and chewing tobacco.
  5. Chronic inflammatory conditions (lichen sclerosus, balanitis).

Protective factor: circumcision in childhood and good hygiene. It presents as a painless warty or ulcerated growth and spreads to inguinal lymph nodes.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Clinical Pathology: Body Fluids, Urine and Faeces
question: Explain semen analysis – collection of the sample, normal values and its importance in infertility.
answer_html:
Introduction Semen analysis (seminogram) is the laboratory examination of ejaculated semen to assess male fertility. Male factors contribute to about 40–50% of infertility in couples, so semen analysis is one of the first tests in infertility evaluation and is also done to confirm success after vasectomy.

1. Collection of the sample – instructions to the patient

  1. Sexual abstinence for 2–7 days before collection.
  2. Collect by masturbation into a clean, dry, sterile, wide-mouthed container provided by the laboratory – not in an ordinary condom (contains spermicide/lubricant) and not by withdrawal (first part, richest in sperm, may be lost).
  3. Collect the complete ejaculate; inform staff if any portion is lost.
  4. Deliver to the laboratory within 30–60 minutes, keeping the container at body temperature (close to the body, not in the fridge).
  5. Label with name, date, time of collection and period of abstinence.
  6. Two samples, a few weeks apart, are usually needed because results vary.

2. Parameters examined

  • Macroscopic: volume, appearance (grey-white, opalescent), liquefaction (within 15–60 minutes), viscosity, pH (7.2 or more).
  • Microscopic: sperm concentration and total count, motility (progressive, non-progressive, immotile), morphology (head, midpiece, tail defects), vitality, round cells and pus cells, agglutination.
  • Additional tests: fructose (absent in obstruction of seminal vesicles/ejaculatory ducts), antisperm antibodies, DNA fragmentation, culture.

3. Normal (lower reference) values – WHO | Parameter | Lower reference limit | |---|---| | Volume | About 1.4–1.5 mL | | Sperm concentration | About 15–16 million/mL | | Total sperm count | About 39 million per ejaculate | | Total motility | About 40–42% | | Progressive motility | About 30–32% | | Normal morphology (strict criteria) | 4% | | Vitality (live sperm) | About 54–58% | | pH | 7.2 or more | | White cells | Less than 1 million/mL |

4. Terms used in reporting

  • Normozoospermia – all values normal.
  • Oligozoospermia – low sperm concentration; azoospermia – no sperm in the ejaculate; aspermia – no ejaculate.
  • Asthenozoospermia – reduced motility; teratozoospermia – abnormal morphology; necrozoospermia – dead sperm; leucocytospermia – excess white cells (infection).

5. Importance in infertility

  • Identifies male-factor infertility and its type – obstructive (e.g. after infection, congenital absence of vas) or non-obstructive (testicular failure, varicocele, undescended testes, hormonal and genetic causes such as Klinefelter syndrome).
  • Guides treatment – lifestyle change, treatment of infection/varicocele, hormonal therapy, intrauterine insemination (IUI), IVF or ICSI.
  • After vasectomy (NSV) – semen is examined at about 3 months; the couple must use another contraceptive until azoospermia is confirmed.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses give clear, private and sensitive instructions; poor collection technique is the commonest cause of falsely abnormal results.
  • Counselling reduces anxiety and stigma; men should be encouraged to take part in infertility evaluation, not only women.

Conclusion Semen analysis measures volume, sperm count, motility and morphology against WHO reference values. Correct collection and timely transport are essential for reliable results that guide the management of male infertility and confirm vasectomy success.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Clinical Pathology: Body Fluids, Urine and Faeces
question: Explain the laboratory examination of faeces (stool) and the significance of the findings.
answer_html:
Introduction Stool (faecal) examination is a simple, cheap and very useful test in India, where intestinal parasites, diarrhoeal diseases and gastrointestinal bleeding are common. It includes macroscopic, microscopic and chemical examination, and culture when needed.

1. Macroscopic examination

  • Colour:
    • Black tarry (melaena) – upper GI bleeding; also iron or bismuth intake (not sticky).
    • Bright red blood – lower GI bleeding, haemorrhoids, dysentery.
    • Clay-coloured/pale – obstructive jaundice; greasy, bulky, foul, floating – fat malabsorption (steatorrhoea).
    • Rice-water stools – cholera.
  • Consistency: formed, semi-formed, liquid.
  • Mucus and blood – dysentery (amoebic, bacillary), inflammatory bowel disease.
  • Visible worms or segments – Ascaris, Enterobius, tapeworm proglottids.

2. Microscopic examination

  • Saline and iodine wet mounts:
    • Ova (eggs) of helminths – roundworm (Ascaris), hookworm, whipworm (Trichuris), dwarf tapeworm (H. nana), Taenia.
    • Cysts and trophozoites of protozoa – Entamoeba histolytica (trophozoites with ingested RBCs in amoebic dysentery), Giardia (pear-shaped trophozoites, oval cysts).
  • Pus cells and RBCs – many pus cells suggest bacillary dysentery (Shigella) or invasive infection.
  • Fat globules (Sudan stain), undigested muscle fibres and starch – malabsorption.
  • Charcot–Leyden crystals – amoebiasis, parasitic infections.
  • Concentration methods (formol–ether) increase the chance of finding scanty ova and cysts.

3. Chemical examination

  • Occult blood test – detects hidden blood (guaiac or immunochemical tests); positive in hookworm infestation, peptic ulcer, colorectal cancer, ulcerative colitis; used for colorectal cancer screening. Avoid red meat, iron and vitamin C before guaiac tests.
  • Reducing substances – sugars in stool in carbohydrate (lactose) intolerance, especially in infants after diarrhoea.
  • Stool pH – acidic (below 5.5) in carbohydrate malabsorption.
  • Faecal fat estimation – steatorrhoea.

4. Other tests

  • Stool culture – Salmonella, Shigella, Vibrio cholerae (TCBS medium), Campylobacter.
  • Antigen tests – rotavirus, Giardia, H. pylori stool antigen; Clostridioides difficile toxin in antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.
  • Faecal calprotectin – inflammatory bowel disease.
  • Hanging-drop – darting motility of V. cholerae.

5. Sample requirements

  • Fresh sample, free from urine and water, in a clean wide-mouthed container; liquid stool examined within 30 minutes for motile trophozoites.
  • Three samples on separate days for ova and cysts, because parasites are shed intermittently.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Correct collection and prompt delivery decide whether parasites are detected; nurses also explain diet restrictions before occult blood tests.
  • Positive findings guide deworming (albendazole), antiprotozoal treatment, ORS and hygiene education, important in schools and anganwadis.

Conclusion Stool examination – macroscopic, microscopic, chemical and culture – detects parasites, infections, bleeding and malabsorption. Fresh, properly collected samples and repeated examinations increase its diagnostic value.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Clinical Pathology: Body Fluids, Urine and Faeces
question: Explain urine culture and sensitivity testing and the interpretation of results.
answer_html:
Introduction Urine culture and sensitivity (C&S) identifies the organism causing a urinary tract infection (UTI), counts it, and finds which antibiotics it is sensitive or resistant to. With rising antimicrobial resistance in India, culture-guided treatment is essential, especially in complicated, recurrent, hospital-acquired and pregnancy-related UTIs.

1. Indications

  • Symptoms of UTI in men, children, pregnant women, the elderly, and in catheterised or diabetic patients.
  • Recurrent or treatment-failure UTI, pyelonephritis, urosepsis, fever without a focus in infants.
  • Screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy and before urological surgery.

2. Sample

  • Clean-catch midstream urine in a sterile container; catheter port sample (not from the bag) in catheterised patients; suprapubic aspiration in infants when needed.
  • Collect before starting antibiotics; send within 1–2 hours or refrigerate at 4°C (up to about 24 hours) or use boric-acid containers.

3. Laboratory procedure

  1. Screening tests: dipstick for nitrite (Gram-negative bacteria convert nitrate to nitrite) and leucocyte esterase (pus cells); microscopy for pyuria (more than 5 pus cells per high-power field in centrifuged urine) and bacteria; Gram stain of uncentrifuged urine.
  2. Semi-quantitative culture: a calibrated loop (0.001 or 0.01 mL) is used to inoculate CLED agar or blood agar and MacConkey agar; incubated overnight at 37°C.
  3. Colony count is calculated as colony-forming units (CFU) per mL.
  4. Identification of the organism by biochemical tests or automated systems.
  5. Antibiotic sensitivity testing – Kirby–Bauer disc diffusion (zone of inhibition) or automated MIC methods; reported as Sensitive (S), Intermediate (I) or Resistant (R); screening for ESBL and carbapenem resistance.
  6. Report usually available in 48–72 hours.

4. Interpretation of results

  • Significant bacteriuria (Kass criteria): 10⁵ CFU/mL or more of a single organism in a midstream sample indicates true infection.
  • Lower counts (10³–10⁴ CFU/mL) may be significant in symptomatic women, men and catheterised patients; any growth in a suprapubic sample is significant.
  • Mixed growth of three or more organisms – usually contamination; repeat the sample.
  • No growth with pus cells (sterile pyuria) – partially treated UTI, urinary tuberculosis (send for AFB/NAAT), stones, chlamydia, interstitial nephritis.
  • Common organisms: E. coli (most common), Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus, Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus saprophyticus (young women), Candida (catheterised/diabetic patients).

5. Uses of the report

  • Choice of the narrowest effective antibiotic; change of empirical therapy; surveillance of local resistance patterns (antibiogram).

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Teaching the correct midstream technique (clean the area, discard first part, collect midstream) and avoiding samples from the urine bag prevent contaminated, misleading reports.
  • Nurses should follow up reports and inform the doctor promptly when the organism is resistant to the antibiotic being given.

Conclusion Urine C&S confirms UTI by detecting significant bacteriuria (10⁵ CFU/mL or more in a midstream sample), identifies the organism and its antibiotic sensitivity. Proper sample collection and careful interpretation ensure correct, targeted treatment.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Clinical Pathology: Body Fluids, Urine and Faeces
question: Explain the examination of sputum and its diagnostic significance.
answer_html:
Introduction Sputum is the secretion coughed up from the lower respiratory tract. Its examination helps in the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis, pneumonia, lung abscess, bronchiectasis, asthma and lung cancer. In India, sputum testing is the backbone of TB diagnosis under the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP).

1. Collection

  • Early-morning sample after rinsing the mouth with water (not toothpaste), obtained by deep cough – sputum, not saliva.
  • Wide-mouthed, sterile, screw-capped container; two samples (spot and early morning) for TB; induced sputum (hypertonic saline) when the patient cannot expectorate.
  • Collect in open air or a well-ventilated area away from others; transport promptly.

2. Macroscopic examination | Appearance | Suggests | |---|---| | Mucoid, white | Chronic bronchitis, asthma | | Purulent (yellow/green) | Bacterial infection, bronchiectasis | | Rusty | Lobar (pneumococcal) pneumonia | | Red-currant jelly | Klebsiella pneumonia | | Pink, frothy | Acute pulmonary oedema | | Blood-streaked or frank blood (haemoptysis) | Tuberculosis, lung cancer, bronchiectasis | | Foul-smelling, copious, layering on standing | Lung abscess, bronchiectasis (anaerobes) | | Anchovy-sauce | Amoebic liver abscess rupturing into the lung |

3. Microscopic examination

  • Gram stain – identifies bacteria (Gram-positive diplococci in pneumococcal pneumonia); also checks sample quality (many pus cells and few epithelial cells = good sample).
  • Ziehl–Neelsen or fluorescent (auramine) stain – acid-fast bacilli of M. tuberculosis; graded as scanty, 1+, 2+, 3+.
  • KOH mount – fungi (Aspergillus, Candida).
  • Eosinophils, Charcot–Leyden crystals and Curschmann's spirals – bronchial asthma.
  • "Heart failure cells" (haemosiderin-laden macrophages) – chronic venous congestion of lungs (mitral stenosis).
  • Cytology (Papanicolaou stain) – malignant cells in lung cancer; three consecutive early-morning samples increase yield.

4. Molecular and culture tests

  • Cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test (CBNAAT/GeneXpert) and Truenat – detect M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance in about 2 hours; recommended as the first test for presumptive TB under NTEP.
  • Culture – bacterial culture and sensitivity for pneumonia; liquid (MGIT) and solid (LJ) culture with drug-susceptibility testing for TB.
  • Line probe assay for drug resistance.

5. Diagnostic significance

  • Confirms TB and drug resistance; identifies the cause of pneumonia and guides antibiotics; supports diagnosis of asthma, lung abscess, bronchiectasis, pulmonary oedema and lung cancer; used to monitor response to TB treatment (follow-up sputum).

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses teach the patient to produce a deep-cough sample, ensure cough hygiene and infection control during collection, label and send samples promptly, and follow up results for timely treatment initiation and notification of TB.

Conclusion Sputum examination – appearance, microscopy, molecular tests, culture and cytology – provides key information in respiratory diseases. Good collection technique and prompt processing make it one of the most valuable tests for TB control in India.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Clinical Pathology: Body Fluids, Urine and Faeces
question: Explain the examination of body cavity fluids – pleural, peritoneal (ascitic) and synovial fluids – and the significance of the findings.
answer_html:
Introduction The pleural, peritoneal and pericardial cavities and the joints normally contain only a small amount of fluid. Abnormal accumulation (effusion) is examined after thoracentesis, paracentesis or arthrocentesis to find the cause – infection, tuberculosis, malignancy, heart, liver or kidney disease. (Transudate–exudate differences and CSF examination are dealt with in Pathology I.)

1. Collection

  • Aspirated under aseptic conditions by the doctor; the nurse prepares the patient, assists and sends samples in:
    • Plain sterile tube – biochemistry, ADA.
    • EDTA tube – total and differential cell count.
    • Fluoride tube – glucose.
    • Sterile container/blood-culture bottles (bedside) – culture, Gram stain, AFB, NAAT.
    • Large volume in a clean container – cytology for malignant cells.
  • Label and send immediately.

2. Tests performed

  • Physical: volume, colour (straw, blood-stained, turbid, milky), clotting.
  • Biochemical: protein, albumin, glucose, LDH, adenosine deaminase (ADA), amylase, triglycerides.
  • Cells: total count and differential (neutrophils vs lymphocytes).
  • Microbiology: Gram stain, culture, AFB stain, CBNAAT for TB.
  • Cytology: malignant cells.

3. Pleural fluid – significance

  • Lymphocyte-rich exudate with high ADA (above about 40 U/L) – tuberculous effusion (very common in India).
  • Neutrophil-rich, low glucose, low pH, positive culture or pus – empyema / parapneumonic effusion.
  • Blood-stained with malignant cells – malignant effusion (lung, breast cancer, lymphoma).
  • Milky fluid with high triglycerides – chylothorax.

4. Peritoneal (ascitic) fluid – significance

  • Serum–ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) = serum albumin – ascitic albumin:
    • SAAG 1.1 g/dL or more – portal hypertension (cirrhosis, heart failure, Budd–Chiari syndrome).
    • SAAG less than 1.1 g/dL – tuberculous peritonitis, malignancy, pancreatitis, nephrotic syndrome.
  • Neutrophils 250 cells/mm³ or more – spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in cirrhosis – needs urgent antibiotics.
  • High ADA, lymphocytes – abdominal tuberculosis; high amylase – pancreatic ascites; malignant cells – peritoneal carcinomatosis (ovary, stomach).

5. Synovial (joint) fluid – significance | Type | Appearance and cells | Causes | |---|---|---| | Normal | Clear, highly viscous; fewer than 200 WBC/mm³ | – | | Non-inflammatory | Clear, viscous; fewer than 2,000 WBC | Osteoarthritis, trauma | | Inflammatory | Cloudy, less viscous; 2,000–50,000 WBC | Rheumatoid arthritis, gout | | Septic | Turbid/purulent; often more than 50,000 WBC, mostly neutrophils; organisms on Gram stain/culture | Septic arthritis – emergency | | Haemorrhagic | Blood | Trauma, haemophilia | - Crystals under polarised light: needle-shaped monosodium urate (gout); rhomboid calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout).

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Correct tubes and prompt dispatch prevent false results; after aspiration, nurses monitor for hypotension (large-volume paracentesis), pneumothorax (thoracentesis), bleeding and infection.

Conclusion Analysis of pleural, ascitic and synovial fluids – appearance, cells, biochemistry (SAAG, ADA, glucose), microbiology and cytology – identifies tuberculosis, infections, malignancy and systemic diseases, guiding prompt treatment.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Clinical Pathology: Body Fluids, Urine and Faeces
question: Write the normal values of semen analysis.
answer_html:
Normal semen values (WHO lower reference limits)

  1. Volume: about 1.4–1.5 mL or more.
  2. pH: 7.2 or more; liquefaction within 15–60 minutes.
  3. Sperm concentration: about 15–16 million/mL or more; total count about 39 million per ejaculate or more.
  4. Total motility: about 40–42% or more; progressive motility about 30–32% or more.
  5. Normal morphology: 4% or more (strict criteria).
  6. Vitality: about 54–58% live sperm or more.
  7. White cells: less than 1 million/mL.

Values below these suggest oligozoospermia, asthenozoospermia or teratozoospermia; absence of sperm is azoospermia.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Clinical Pathology: Body Fluids, Urine and Faeces
question: What is significant bacteriuria?
answer_html:
Significant bacteriuria is the presence of bacteria in urine in numbers that indicate true infection rather than contamination during collection.

  • Kass criteria: 10⁵ (1,00,000) or more colony-forming units (CFU) per mL of a single organism in a properly collected clean-catch midstream urine sample.
  • Lower counts (10³–10⁴ CFU/mL) may be significant in symptomatic women, men and catheter samples; any growth in a suprapubic aspirate is significant.
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria – significant bacteriuria without symptoms; it must be treated in pregnancy because it can lead to pyelonephritis and preterm labour.
  • Mixed growth of several organisms usually means contamination – repeat the sample.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Clinical Pathology: Body Fluids, Urine and Faeces
question: What are reducing substances in stool? Write their significance.
answer_html:
Reducing substances are sugars (lactose, glucose, galactose) present in stool when carbohydrates are not digested or absorbed in the small intestine.

  • Test: fresh liquid stool is tested with Benedict's reagent/Clinitest tablets; more than 0.5% is positive (0.25–0.5% trace); stool pH is usually acidic (below 5.5).
  • Significance:
    1. Lactose intolerance – temporary after acute gastroenteritis (e.g. rotavirus) in infants; congenital lactase deficiency (rare).
    2. Other disaccharidase deficiencies (sucrase–isomaltase) and glucose–galactose malabsorption.
    3. Mucosal damage – coeliac disease, severe malnutrition.
  • Helps decide on a temporary lactose-free or low-lactose diet in persistent diarrhoea while continuing breastfeeding.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Pathology II – Clinical Pathology: Body Fluids, Urine and Faeces
question: What is the adenosine deaminase (ADA) test? Write its significance.
answer_html:
Adenosine deaminase (ADA) is an enzyme of purine metabolism found mainly in activated T-lymphocytes and macrophages. Its level in body fluids rises when there is a strong cell-mediated immune response, as in tuberculosis.

Significance

  1. Pleural fluid ADA above about 40 U/L in a lymphocytic exudate strongly suggests tuberculous pleural effusion.
  2. Raised ADA in ascitic fluid (abdominal TB), pericardial fluid (TB pericarditis) and CSF (tuberculous meningitis, above about 10 U/L).
  3. It is cheap, rapid and widely available, very useful in India where TB is common and fluid culture is slow.
  4. False positives – empyema, lymphoma, rheumatoid effusions; results are interpreted with clinical features and NAAT/culture.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics I – Introduction: Nature, Principles and Perspectives of Heredity
question: Explain the patterns of single-gene (Mendelian) inheritance with their characteristics and examples.

diagram.caption: Pedigree patterns of single-gene inheritance
labels: autosomal dominant – affected in every generation
male-to-male transmission; autosomal recessive – affected siblings of unaffected carrier parents
often consanguinity; X-linked recessive – affected males related through carrier females
no male-to-male transmission; mitochondrial – transmitted only through mothers

answer_html:
Introduction Gregor Johann Mendel (1822–1884), the "father of genetics", discovered the basic laws of heredity by experiments on garden peas. Disorders caused by a mutation in a single gene follow these simple Mendelian patterns and can be recognised by studying a family tree (pedigree).

1. Mendel's laws

  1. Law of dominance – of two different alleles, one (dominant) expresses itself and masks the other (recessive).
  2. Law of segregation – the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one.
  3. Law of independent assortment – genes for different traits (on different chromosomes) are inherited independently.

2. Autosomal dominant (AD) inheritance

  • One copy of the abnormal gene is enough to cause disease.
  • Affected persons in every generation (vertical pattern); males and females equally affected; male-to-male transmission occurs.
  • An affected parent has a 50% chance of passing it to each child; unaffected members do not transmit it (unless penetrance is incomplete).
  • Variable expressivity and new mutations are common.
  • Examples: Huntington's disease, achondroplasia, Marfan syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1, familial hypercholesterolaemia, adult polycystic kidney disease, hereditary spherocytosis, BRCA1/2 hereditary breast–ovarian cancer.

3. Autosomal recessive (AR) inheritance

  • Two copies (one from each parent) are needed; carriers (heterozygotes) are healthy.
  • Usually seen in siblings of unaffected parents (horizontal pattern); males and females equally affected.
  • Two carrier parents: 25% affected, 50% carriers, 25% normal with each pregnancy.
  • More common with consanguineous marriage.
  • Examples: sickle cell anaemia, β-thalassaemia, cystic fibrosis, phenylketonuria, albinism, galactosaemia, Wilson's disease, spinal muscular atrophy, most inborn errors of metabolism.

4. X-linked recessive inheritance

  • Gene on the X chromosome; mostly males affected (they have only one X).
  • Transmitted through carrier females; no male-to-male transmission.
  • Carrier mother: 50% of sons affected, 50% of daughters carriers. Affected father: all daughters carriers, all sons normal.
  • Examples: haemophilia A and B, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, G6PD deficiency, red–green colour blindness.

5. X-linked dominant inheritance

  • Affected father transmits to all daughters and no sons; affected mother to half of her children.
  • Examples: hypophosphataemic (vitamin D-resistant) rickets, Rett syndrome.

6. Y-linked (holandric) inheritance

  • Only males; passed from father to all sons – e.g. some Y-chromosome microdeletions causing male infertility.

7. Mitochondrial inheritance

  • Mitochondrial DNA comes only from the ovum, so it is passed from the mother to all her children; fathers do not transmit it.
  • Examples: Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy, MELAS.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Drawing a three-generation pedigree helps nurses identify inheritance patterns, recurrence risks and family members who need screening or counselling.
  • Knowledge of AR inheritance underlies carrier screening for sickle cell disease and thalassaemia, very important in central India.

Conclusion Single-gene disorders follow autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, Y-linked or mitochondrial patterns, each with typical pedigree features and recurrence risks. Recognising these patterns is the basis of genetic counselling and prevention.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics I – Introduction: Nature, Principles and Perspectives of Heredity
question: Describe the structure and classification of chromosomes. Explain karyotyping and sex determination.

diagram.caption: Structure of a metaphase chromosome
labels: two sister chromatids joined at the centromere

answer_html:
Introduction Chromosomes are thread-like structures in the nucleus made of DNA wound around histone proteins (chromatin). They carry the genes. Human body cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) – 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX in females, XY in males); gametes have 23.

1. Structure of a chromosome (seen best in metaphase)

  • Two sister chromatids joined at the centromere (primary constriction).
  • Short arm (p) and long arm (q).
  • Telomeres – protective ends that shorten with ageing.
  • Satellites – small knobs on the short arms of acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22).
  • Kinetochore – attachment site for spindle fibres during cell division.

2. Classification a) By position of centromere

  • Metacentric – centromere in the middle (e.g. chromosomes 1, 3).
  • Submetacentric – slightly off-centre (most chromosomes, e.g. 4–12, X).
  • Acrocentric – near one end (13–15, 21, 22, Y).
  • Telocentric – at the end (not found in humans).

b) Denver/ISCN grouping by size and shape

  • Group A (1–3), B (4–5), C (6–12 and X), D (13–15), E (16–18), F (19–20), G (21–22 and Y).

3. Karyotyping

  • Definition: the systematic arrangement of a person's chromosomes (photographed at metaphase) in pairs by size, centromere position and banding pattern.
  • Steps:
    1. Culture of lymphocytes from peripheral blood (or amniotic cells, chorionic villi, bone marrow) with phytohaemagglutinin to stimulate division.
    2. Colchicine to arrest cells in metaphase.
    3. Hypotonic solution to swell cells and spread chromosomes; fixation and slide preparation.
    4. G-banding (Giemsa staining) to produce band patterns; photography or digital imaging and arrangement.
  • Written as: normal female 46,XX; normal male 46,XY; Down syndrome male 47,XY,+21.
  • Uses: diagnosis of chromosomal disorders (Down, Turner, Klinefelter), recurrent miscarriage and infertility, ambiguous genitalia, prenatal diagnosis, leukaemias (e.g. Philadelphia chromosome in CML).

4. Sex determination

  • The ovum always carries an X; the sperm carries either X or Y – so the father's sperm determines the sex of the baby.
  • XX → female; XY → male.
  • The SRY gene (sex-determining region Y) on the Y chromosome produces testis-determining factor → testes develop (about 7th week) → testosterone and anti-Müllerian hormone produce male internal and external organs; without SRY, female development occurs.
  • Barr body (sex chromatin): in females one X is inactivated (Lyon hypothesis) and appears as a dark body at the nuclear membrane; number of Barr bodies = number of X chromosomes minus one (none in Turner 45,X; one in Klinefelter 47,XXY).

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses can correct the harmful belief, common in Indian families, that the mother is responsible for the birth of daughters – sex is decided by the father's sperm; sex selection is a crime under the PCPNDT Act.
