  • Nurses collect blood or prenatal samples correctly for karyotyping and explain the test to families.

Conclusion Human cells contain 46 chromosomes, each with two chromatids joined at a centromere and classified by size and centromere position. Karyotyping arranges them to detect abnormalities, and sex is determined at fertilisation by the X- or Y-bearing sperm through the SRY gene.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics I – Introduction: Nature, Principles and Perspectives of Heredity
question: Explain chromosomal aberrations – numerical and structural – with examples.
answer_html:
Definition Chromosomal aberrations are abnormalities in the number or structure of chromosomes. They are found in about 50% of first-trimester miscarriages and about 1 in 150 live births, and are important causes of birth defects, intellectual disability and infertility.

A. Numerical aberrations 1. Aneuploidy – gain or loss of one or a few chromosomes (not an exact multiple of 23).

  • Trisomy (47 chromosomes):
    • Trisomy 21 – Down syndrome (most common viable autosomal trisomy).
    • Trisomy 18 – Edwards syndrome – clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, heart defects; most die in infancy.
    • Trisomy 13 – Patau syndrome – cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, holoprosencephaly, microphthalmia; very short survival.
    • 47,XXY – Klinefelter syndrome – tall male, small testes, infertility, gynaecomastia.
    • 47,XXX and 47,XYY – often mild features.
  • Monosomy (45 chromosomes):
    • 45,X – Turner syndrome (the only viable monosomy) – short stature, webbed neck, streak ovaries, primary amenorrhoea, coarctation of aorta.
    • Autosomal monosomies are lethal.

2. Polyploidy – complete extra sets (triploidy 69, tetraploidy 92); usually result in miscarriage or partial mole.

3. Mosaicism – two cell lines with different chromosome numbers in one person (e.g. mosaic Down syndrome) – usually milder features.

Mechanism: mainly non-disjunction – failure of chromosomes to separate during meiosis (more common with advanced maternal age) or mitosis (mosaicism); also anaphase lag.

B. Structural aberrations

  1. Deletion – loss of part of a chromosome:
    • Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion) – cat-like cry, microcephaly, intellectual disability.
    • Microdeletions – 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge syndrome), Prader–Willi/Angelman (15q11–13), Williams syndrome.
  2. Duplication – extra copy of a segment.
  3. Inversion – a segment reversed; carrier is usually normal but may produce abnormal gametes.
  4. Translocation – exchange of segments between chromosomes:
    • Reciprocal – e.g. t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukaemia (BCR-ABL fusion gene).
    • Robertsonian – fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes, e.g. t(14;21), a cause of translocation Down syndrome; balanced carriers are healthy but at risk of abnormal offspring.
  5. Ring chromosome and isochromosome (e.g. isochromosome Xq in some Turner syndrome).

C. Effects of chromosomal aberrations

  • Spontaneous abortion and stillbirth, multiple congenital anomalies, intellectual disability, growth problems, infertility and recurrent miscarriage (balanced translocation carriers), and cancers (acquired changes in tumour cells).

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Couples with recurrent miscarriage or a child with a chromosomal disorder should be referred for karyotyping and genetic counselling; nurses support families emotionally and explain recurrence risks.
  • Prenatal screening is especially advised for women aged 35 years or more.

Conclusion Chromosomal aberrations may be numerical (trisomies, monosomies, polyploidy, mosaicism – mostly due to non-disjunction) or structural (deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations). They cause miscarriage, birth defects, intellectual disability, infertility and some cancers.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics I – Introduction: Nature, Principles and Perspectives of Heredity
question: Define mutation. Explain the types, causes and significance of mutations.
answer_html:
Definition A mutation is a permanent, heritable change in the DNA sequence of a gene, or in the structure or number of chromosomes. Mutations are the source of genetic variation, and also the basis of genetic diseases and cancer.

1. Types of mutations A. According to the cells affected

  • Germline mutations – in eggs or sperm; transmitted to offspring (inherited disorders).
  • Somatic mutations – in body cells; not inherited; cause cancers and mosaicism.

B. According to the extent of change

  1. Gene (point) mutations – change in one or a few nucleotides:
    • Substitution – one base replaced by another:
      • Silent – codes for the same amino acid; no effect.
      • Missense – codes for a different amino acid, e.g. sickle cell anaemia (GAG → GTG; glutamic acid replaced by valine at position 6 of β-globin).
      • Nonsense – creates a stop codon → short, non-functional protein (some β-thalassaemias, Duchenne muscular dystrophy).
    • Frameshift – insertion or deletion of bases (not in multiples of three) shifts the reading frame → completely altered protein (e.g. Tay–Sachs disease).
    • Splice-site mutations – abnormal RNA processing (common in β-thalassaemia).
  2. Trinucleotide repeat expansions (dynamic mutations) – repeats increase over generations, causing earlier and more severe disease (anticipation) – Huntington's disease (CAG), fragile X syndrome (CGG), myotonic dystrophy.
  3. Chromosomal mutations – deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations.
  4. Genomic mutations – change in chromosome number (aneuploidy, e.g. trisomy 21).

C. According to effect on function

  • Loss-of-function, gain-of-function, dominant-negative and lethal mutations; some are beneficial (e.g. sickle cell trait protects against severe malaria).

2. Causes

  • Spontaneous – errors in DNA replication, chemical changes in bases.
  • Induced (by mutagens):
    • Physical – ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays, radioactive fallout), ultraviolet rays (thymine dimers → skin cancer).
    • Chemical – tobacco smoke, benzene, alkylating anticancer drugs, nitrosamines, aflatoxins, some pesticides.
    • Biological – viruses inserting into DNA (HPV, hepatitis B).
  • Age-related – increased mutations in older fathers' sperm.

3. Significance

  • Genetic diseases – single-gene disorders, chromosomal syndromes.
  • Cancer – accumulation of somatic mutations in oncogenes and tumour-suppressor genes.
  • Drug resistance – in TB bacilli, HIV and malaria parasites.
  • Evolution and variation – source of genetic diversity.
  • Diagnosis – basis of genetic testing and targeted therapy.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses reduce exposure to mutagens – radiation protection (lead aprons, avoiding unnecessary X-rays especially in pregnancy), safe handling of cytotoxic drugs, and anti-tobacco education.

Conclusion Mutations are permanent changes in DNA, ranging from single-base substitutions and frameshifts to repeat expansions and chromosomal changes. They may be spontaneous or caused by radiation, chemicals and viruses, and underlie genetic diseases, cancer and drug resistance.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics I – Introduction: Nature, Principles and Perspectives of Heredity
question: Explain sex-linked inheritance with examples.
answer_html:
Definition Sex-linked inheritance is the inheritance of traits whose genes are located on the sex chromosomes (X or Y). Because males have only one X chromosome (XY) and females have two (XX), the pattern of transmission differs between the sexes. Most sex-linked disorders are X-linked recessive.

1. X-linked recessive inheritance – features

  • Males are mainly affected – one abnormal X is enough (hemizygous).
  • Females are usually carriers (one normal and one abnormal X); they are affected only if both X chromosomes carry the gene.
  • No male-to-male (father-to-son) transmission, because a father gives his Y to his son.
  • The gene passes from an affected man through his carrier daughters to his grandsons – "criss-cross" or "knight's move" inheritance.

2. Typical crosses (h = abnormal gene) | Parents | Sons | Daughters | |---|---|---| | Carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) × normal father (XᴴY) | 50% affected, 50% normal | 50% carriers, 50% normal | | Normal mother (XᴴXᴴ) × affected father (XʰY) | All normal | All carriers | | Carrier mother × affected father | 50% affected | 50% affected, 50% carriers |

3. Examples of X-linked recessive disorders

  • Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) and B (factor IX) – bleeding into joints and muscles; called the "royal disease" because it spread through Queen Victoria's descendants.
  • Duchenne muscular dystrophy – progressive muscle weakness in boys from 3–5 years, Gowers' sign, calf pseudohypertrophy; wheelchair-bound by early teens.
  • G6PD deficiency – common in parts of India; haemolysis with primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, fava beans; neonatal jaundice.
  • Red–green colour blindness – common in men.
  • X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, Lesch–Nyhan syndrome, fragile X syndrome (complex X-linked pattern).

4. X-linked dominant inheritance

  • Affected father → all daughters affected, no sons; affected mother → half of sons and daughters.
  • Examples: hypophosphataemic (vitamin D-resistant) rickets, Rett syndrome (mostly girls).

5. Y-linked inheritance

  • Genes on the Y chromosome passed only from father to all sons – e.g. Y-chromosome microdeletions causing azoospermia (can be transmitted to sons through ICSI).

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Carrier testing of female relatives (e.g. sisters of a haemophilia patient) and prenatal diagnosis help families make informed choices.
  • Nurses teach G6PD-deficient patients the drugs and foods to avoid, and care for haemophilia patients (factor replacement, joint protection, avoiding IM injections).

Conclusion Sex-linked disorders, mostly X-linked recessive, affect males and are transmitted by carrier females without father-to-son transmission. Haemophilia, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, G6PD deficiency and colour blindness are classic examples.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics I – Introduction: Nature, Principles and Perspectives of Heredity
question: Explain multiple alleles with special reference to the inheritance of blood groups.
answer_html:
Definition Multiple alleles are more than two alternative forms of a gene at the same locus present in a population. Each individual, however, carries only two of them (one on each homologous chromosome). The ABO blood group is the best example.

1. ABO blood group system

  • Controlled by a gene on chromosome 9 with three alleles – Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i (Iᴼ).
  • Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant (both expressed together); both are dominant over i.
  • Genotypes and phenotypes: | Blood group (phenotype) | Possible genotypes | Antigen on RBC | Antibody in plasma | |---|---|---|---| | A | IᴬIᴬ, Iᴬi | A | Anti-B | | B | IᴮIᴮ, Iᴮi | B | Anti-A | | AB | IᴬIᴮ | A and B | None (universal recipient) | | O | ii | None | Anti-A and anti-B (universal donor of red cells) |
  • Six genotypes produce four phenotypes.

2. Examples of inheritance

  • Group A (Iᴬi) × group B (Iᴮi) → children can be A, B, AB or O (25% each).
  • AB × O → children A or B only (never AB or O).
  • O × O → only O.
  • AB × AB → A (25%), AB (50%), B (25%).
  • Such patterns help in excluding (not proving) paternity in medico-legal cases.

3. Rh blood group

  • The D antigen is inherited as a dominant trait: Rh-positive (DD or Dd), Rh-negative (dd).
  • Rh incompatibility: an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive baby may form anti-D antibodies (after delivery, abortion or bleeding) → haemolytic disease of the newborn in later pregnancies; prevented by anti-D immunoglobulin.

4. Bombay blood group (Oh)

  • Persons with genotype hh cannot make the H antigen (precursor of A and B antigens), so they test like group O but have anti-H antibodies.
  • First described in Mumbai (Bombay) in 1952; rare (about 1 in 10,000 Indians); such patients can receive only Bombay blood.

5. Other examples of multiple alleles

  • HLA (human leucocyte antigen) system – very many alleles; important in organ and bone-marrow transplant matching.
  • Rabbit coat colour, eye colour in Drosophila (classical examples).

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Understanding ABO and Rh inheritance helps nurses explain blood transfusion safety, the need for antenatal blood grouping and anti-D prophylaxis, and the possibility of different blood groups among siblings.

Conclusion The ABO gene with three alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i) shows multiple allelism and codominance, producing four blood groups from six genotypes. Rh and Bombay groups add clinical importance for transfusion, pregnancy and transplant care.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics I – Introduction: Nature, Principles and Perspectives of Heredity
question: Explain the application of human genetics in nursing and the impact of genetic conditions on families.
answer_html:
Introduction Genetics and genomics now influence every area of health care – from prenatal care and newborn screening to cancer, chronic diseases and drug therapy. Nurses, being closest to patients and families, are expected to identify genetic risks, educate, support and refer.

A. Applications of human genetics in nursing

  1. Family history and pedigree – taking a three-generation family history to identify inherited risks (thalassaemia, sickle cell, haemophilia, early heart disease, cancers).
  2. Preconception and antenatal care – counselling about consanguinity, maternal age, folic acid and teratogens; supporting prenatal screening and diagnosis.
  3. Newborn screening – collecting heel-prick samples and following up abnormal results (hypothyroidism, G6PD deficiency, sickle cell disease).
  4. Carrier screening programmes – e.g. the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023), which screens people in tribal and high-prevalence districts (including Vidarbha) and issues genetic status cards for premarital counselling.
  5. Care of patients with genetic disorders – transfusion and chelation in thalassaemia, crisis prevention in sickle cell disease, factor replacement in haemophilia, developmental support in Down syndrome.
  6. Cancer genetics – identifying families with BRCA or Lynch syndrome for screening and counselling.
  7. Pharmacogenomics – understanding why drug responses differ, e.g. G6PD deficiency and primaquine, HLA-B*1502 and carbamazepine (Stevens–Johnson syndrome), TPMT and azathioprine.
  8. Genetic counselling support – explaining results, supporting decisions, ensuring confidentiality and informed consent.
  9. Research and ethics – protecting participants' rights in genetic studies.
  10. Community education – reducing stigma and myths about inherited diseases.

B. Impact of genetic conditions on families

  1. Emotional – shock, denial, anxiety, guilt and blame (often unfairly directed at the mother in Indian families), grief for the "expected healthy child".
  2. Social – stigma, isolation, difficulty in marriage arrangements for affected persons, carriers and their siblings.
  3. Financial – cost of lifelong treatment (transfusions, drugs, surgeries), travel and lost wages.
  4. Caregiver burden – physical and mental exhaustion; siblings may feel neglected.
  5. Reproductive decisions – fear about future pregnancies, need for prenatal diagnosis, difficult choices about termination.
  6. Family relationships – marital conflict, dilemmas about disclosing risk to relatives.
  7. Positive effects – stronger family bonds, involvement in support groups and advocacy (e.g. thalassaemia societies).

C. Nurse's supportive role

  • Listen, give accurate information, correct blame, connect families with genetic counselling, support groups, government schemes (free drugs, disability benefits, Rare Diseases Policy support), and coordinate long-term follow-up.

Conclusion Human genetics helps nurses identify risks, screen, educate, care for affected persons and use drugs safely. Genetic conditions affect families emotionally, socially and financially, and nurses play a vital role in support and counselling.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics I – Introduction: Nature, Principles and Perspectives of Heredity
question: Define mutation and enlist its common types.
answer_html:
Mutation is a permanent, heritable change in the nucleotide sequence of DNA (gene) or in the structure or number of chromosomes.

Common types

  1. Germline (inherited) and somatic (not inherited, e.g. cancer) mutations.
  2. Point (gene) mutations – substitution of a base:
    • Silent (no change in amino acid), missense (different amino acid – e.g. sickle cell anaemia), nonsense (premature stop codon).
  3. Frameshift mutations – insertion or deletion of bases.
  4. Trinucleotide repeat expansion – e.g. Huntington's disease, fragile X syndrome.
  5. Chromosomal mutations – deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation.
  6. Genomic mutations – change in chromosome number (aneuploidy, e.g. trisomy 21).

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics I – Introduction: Nature, Principles and Perspectives of Heredity
question: Name two autosomal dominant and two autosomal recessive disorders.
answer_html:
Autosomal dominant disorders (one abnormal copy is enough; 50% risk to each child of an affected parent)

  1. Huntington's disease
  2. Marfan syndrome Others: achondroplasia, neurofibromatosis type 1, familial hypercholesterolaemia, adult polycystic kidney disease.

Autosomal recessive disorders (two abnormal copies needed; carrier parents have a 25% risk with each pregnancy)

  1. Sickle cell anaemia
  2. β-thalassaemia major Others: cystic fibrosis, phenylketonuria, albinism, galactosaemia, Wilson's disease.

Key difference: dominant disorders appear in every generation and can pass from father to son, whereas recessive disorders usually appear in brothers and sisters of healthy carrier parents, more often when the parents are blood relatives.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics I – Introduction: Nature, Principles and Perspectives of Heredity
question: Describe the practical applications of genetics in nursing.
answer_html:
Practical applications of genetics in nursing

  1. Taking family history and drawing pedigrees to identify inherited risks.
  2. Prenatal and newborn screening – explaining tests, collecting samples (heel-prick), following up results.
  3. Carrier screening and premarital counselling – sickle cell disease, thalassaemia.
  4. Care of patients with genetic disorders – thalassaemia, haemophilia, Down syndrome, muscular dystrophy.
  5. Supporting genetic counselling – education, emotional support, informed consent, confidentiality.
  6. Safe drug use (pharmacogenomics) – e.g. avoiding oxidant drugs in G6PD deficiency.
  7. Prevention – periconceptional folic acid, avoiding teratogens and radiation, counselling on consanguinity.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics I – Introduction: Nature, Principles and Perspectives of Heredity
question: What is non-disjunction?
answer_html:
Non-disjunction is the failure of homologous chromosomes (in meiosis I) or sister chromatids (in meiosis II or mitosis) to separate properly during cell division.

  • It produces gametes with an extra or a missing chromosome; after fertilisation the zygote has 47 (trisomy) or 45 (monosomy) chromosomes.
  • Risk increases with maternal age, because primary oocytes remain arrested in prophase of meiosis I from foetal life until ovulation.
  • Examples: about 95% of Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Edwards and Patau syndromes, Turner and Klinefelter syndromes.
  • Non-disjunction in mitosis after fertilisation causes mosaicism.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics I – Introduction: Nature, Principles and Perspectives of Heredity
question: Differentiate between genotype and phenotype.
answer_html:
Genotype Phenotype
The genetic constitution of an individual – the pair of alleles present for a trait The observable characteristics (physical, biochemical or behavioural) of an individual
Inherited from parents; does not change with environment Results from the genotype plus the environment
Written as letters, e.g. AA, Aa, aa; Iᴬi Described as traits, e.g. tall, blood group A, normal skin colour
May not be visible (e.g. a carrier) Visible or measurable

Example: in sickle cell disease – HbAA (normal), HbAS (sickle cell trait – carrier, usually healthy), HbSS (sickle cell anaemia). Homozygous = two identical alleles (AA or aa); heterozygous = two different alleles (Aa).

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics II – Maternal, Prenatal and Genetic Influences on Development of Defects and Diseases
question: Define Down syndrome and describe its causes and clinical features.
answer_html:
Definition Down syndrome is a chromosomal disorder caused by an extra copy (trisomy) of chromosome 21, producing characteristic facial features, intellectual disability, hypotonia and an increased risk of heart and other congenital defects. It is the most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability, occurring in about 1 in 700–800 live births.

1. Causes (cytogenetic types) | Type | Frequency | Mechanism | |---|---|---| | Free trisomy 21 (47,XX/XY,+21) | About 95% | Non-disjunction, mostly in maternal meiosis I; risk rises with maternal age | | Translocation Down syndrome | About 3–4% | Robertsonian translocation, e.g. t(14;21); may be inherited from a balanced carrier parent – higher recurrence risk | | Mosaic Down syndrome | About 1–2% | Non-disjunction in early mitosis; two cell lines; milder features |

Maternal age and risk: about 1 in 1,500 at 20–25 years, 1 in 350 at 35 years, 1 in 100 at 40 years and 1 in 30 at 45 years.

2. Clinical features a) Face and head

  • Flat facial profile, upward-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, Brushfield spots (white spots on the iris).
  • Flat nasal bridge, small low-set ears, protruding tongue (small mouth), small head with flat occiput.
  • Short neck with excess skin at the nape.

b) Hands and feet

  • Single transverse palmar (simian) crease, short broad hands, incurved little finger (clinodactyly).
  • Sandal gap – wide gap between the first and second toes.

c) Neuromuscular and development

  • Generalised hypotonia ("floppy baby"), joint laxity, poor sucking in infancy.
  • Intellectual disability (usually mild to moderate), developmental delay, short stature.
  • Usually cheerful, sociable children.

d) Associated problems

  • Congenital heart disease (40–50%) – atrioventricular septal defect, VSD, ASD, PDA.
  • Gastrointestinal – duodenal atresia ("double bubble"), Hirschsprung's disease, imperforate anus.
  • Hypothyroidism, hearing loss, refractive errors and cataract, recurrent respiratory infections, obstructive sleep apnoea.
  • Leukaemia (10–20 times higher risk), early-onset Alzheimer's disease, atlanto-axial instability.
  • Males are usually infertile; females may conceive.

3. Diagnosis

  • Prenatal screening – combined first-trimester test (nuchal translucency, PAPP-A, free β-hCG), quadruple test, cell-free DNA screening.
  • Confirmation – karyotype (from chorionic villi, amniotic fluid or the baby's blood).

4. Management

  • No cure; multidisciplinary care – cardiac evaluation (echocardiography) and surgery, thyroid and hearing/vision screening, early intervention (physiotherapy, speech therapy, special education) through District Early Intervention Centres (RBSK), inclusive schooling and vocational training.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses help with feeding (hypotonia), prevent infections, encourage developmental stimulation, support parents through grief and acceptance, and arrange genetic counselling (especially to test for translocation carriers).

Conclusion Down syndrome results from trisomy 21, usually due to maternal non-disjunction linked to increasing maternal age. Its typical facial and limb features, hypotonia, intellectual disability and associated heart and gut defects require lifelong multidisciplinary care and family support.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics II – Maternal, Prenatal and Genetic Influences on Development of Defects and Diseases
question: Explain prenatal testing and diagnosis of genetic disorders, with the nurse's role.
answer_html:
Introduction Prenatal testing detects genetic and structural abnormalities in the foetus before birth. It includes screening tests (which estimate risk safely) and diagnostic tests (which confirm the diagnosis but carry a small risk). Results help parents prepare, plan delivery at a suitable centre, or make informed choices under the MTP Act.

1. Indications

  • Maternal age 35 years or more.
  • Previous child with a chromosomal disorder, neural tube defect or genetic disease.
  • Parents known carriers – balanced translocation, thalassaemia, sickle cell disease, haemophilia, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, spinal muscular atrophy.
  • Abnormal screening test or ultrasound finding.
  • Consanguineous couple with family history; exposure to teratogens; recurrent miscarriage.

2. Screening tests (non-invasive)

  • First-trimester combined test (11–13⁺⁶ weeks): nuchal translucency (NT) scan + PAPP-A + free β-hCG ("double marker").
  • Second-trimester quadruple test (15–20 weeks): AFP, hCG, unconjugated oestriol and inhibin A; raised maternal serum AFP suggests open neural tube defect.
  • Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT/cell-free DNA) from maternal blood after 10 weeks – very sensitive for trisomies, but positive results must be confirmed.
  • Ultrasound – dating scan, NT scan, targeted anomaly scan at 18–22 weeks, foetal echocardiography.

3. Diagnostic tests (invasive) | Test | Timing | Sample and uses | Risk | |---|---|---|---| | Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) | 10–13 weeks | Placental tissue – karyotype, DNA tests for thalassaemia/sickle cell | Miscarriage about 0.5–1% | | Amniocentesis | 15–20 weeks | Amniotic fluid cells – karyotype, FISH, microarray, DNA tests; AFP and acetylcholinesterase for NTD | Miscarriage about 0.1–0.5%, leakage, infection | | Cordocentesis | After 18 weeks | Foetal blood – rapid karyotype, foetal anaemia, infections | Higher risk | - Pre-implantation genetic testing of embryos during IVF for known familial disorders.

4. Legal aspects – PCPNDT Act, 1994 (amended 2003)

  • Prenatal diagnostic techniques may be used only for detecting genetic, metabolic, chromosomal and congenital abnormalities, in registered facilities with the woman's written consent and records (e.g. Form F for ultrasound).
  • Determination or disclosure of the sex of the foetus is prohibited and punishable with imprisonment and fine; advertisements for sex selection are banned.

5. Nurse's role

  1. Explain the difference between screening and diagnostic tests, their accuracy and risks, in simple language; ensure informed, voluntary consent.
  2. Provide non-directive counselling support – respect the couple's decisions; maintain confidentiality.
  3. Prepare the woman for procedures – check blood group, explain the procedure, ensure comfort.
  4. After CVS/amniocentesis – observe for pain, bleeding, leakage of fluid and fever; advise rest for 24 hours; give anti-D to Rh-negative women.
  5. Support parents emotionally when results are abnormal and coordinate with obstetricians, paediatricians and genetic counsellors.
  6. Never disclose foetal sex; report violations of the PCPNDT Act.

Conclusion Prenatal testing combines safe screening (NT, biochemical markers, NIPT, anomaly scans) with confirmatory diagnostic procedures (CVS, amniocentesis, cordocentesis). Ethical use within the PCPNDT Act, with informed consent and compassionate counselling, is essential.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics II – Maternal, Prenatal and Genetic Influences on Development of Defects and Diseases
question: Explain the maternal, prenatal and environmental factors that influence the development of birth defects and diseases.
answer_html:
Introduction Birth defects (congenital anomalies) are structural or functional abnormalities present at birth. About 3–6% of babies are born with a significant birth defect. Their causes are genetic, environmental or multifactorial, and many environmental causes act through the mother during pregnancy – which makes them preventable.

1. Maternal genetic conditions and diseases

  • Maternal diabetes (pre-existing, poorly controlled) – heart defects, neural tube defects, caudal regression, macrosomia.
  • Maternal phenylketonuria (uncontrolled) – microcephaly, intellectual disability and heart defects in the baby.
  • Epilepsy (and antiepileptic drugs), hypothyroidism and iodine deficiency (impaired brain development, cretinism), maternal SLE (congenital heart block), obesity.
  • Parental balanced translocations – recurrent miscarriage and abnormal offspring.

2. Maternal infections (TORCH and others)

  • Toxoplasmosis (hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, intracranial calcification).
  • Rubella (congenital rubella syndrome – cataract, deafness, heart defects, microcephaly; highest risk in the first 12 weeks).
  • Cytomegalovirus (deafness, microcephaly) – the commonest congenital infection.
  • Herpes simplex, syphilis, varicella, parvovirus B19, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika (microcephaly), malaria.

3. Consanguinity and atopy

  • Consanguinity (marriage between blood relatives) increases the risk of autosomal recessive disorders and birth defects.
  • Atopy (inherited tendency to allergies) in parents increases the child's risk of asthma, eczema and allergies.

4. Maternal age

  • Teenage mothers – prematurity, low birth weight.
  • 35 years or more – chromosomal disorders (Down syndrome) due to non-disjunction, miscarriage.
  • Older fathers – slightly increased new dominant mutations (e.g. achondroplasia).

5. Prenatal nutrition and food allergies

  • Folic acid deficiency → neural tube defects; iodine deficiency → cretinism; iron deficiency → low birth weight; excess vitamin A → malformations.
  • Maternal undernutrition → growth restriction and higher adult risk of diabetes and heart disease ("foetal origins of adult disease").
  • Avoiding allergenic foods in pregnancy is not recommended for allergy prevention; balanced diet is advised.

6. Maternal drug therapy (teratogens)

  • Thalidomide (limb defects – phocomelia), isotretinoin, valproate and carbamazepine (neural tube defects), phenytoin, warfarin, ACE inhibitors, tetracyclines, methotrexate, misoprostol, lithium.
  • Alcohol (foetal alcohol spectrum disorder), tobacco (low birth weight, cleft lip/palate), recreational drugs.
  • The period of organogenesis (3–8 weeks after conception) is the most sensitive.

7. Radiation, drugs and chemicals

  • High-dose ionising radiation – microcephaly, intellectual disability, growth restriction (routine diagnostic X-rays give much lower doses, but unnecessary exposure is avoided).
  • Chemicals – lead, mercury (Minamata disease), arsenic in groundwater, solvents and pesticides (the endosulfan tragedy in Kasaragod, Kerala, was linked to birth defects); the Bhopal gas disaster increased miscarriages and stillbirths.

8. Prevention

  • Preconception care – folic acid, rubella immunity (MR vaccine), control of diabetes and epilepsy with safer drugs.
  • Avoid teratogens, alcohol, tobacco and unnecessary X-rays; food safety; occupational protection.
  • Genetic counselling for consanguineous couples and carrier screening.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses identify risk factors during preconception and antenatal visits, educate on folic acid, safe medicines and infections, and refer high-risk couples.

Conclusion Birth defects arise from maternal genetic conditions and diseases, infections, consanguinity, maternal age, nutrition, drugs, radiation and chemicals. Many of these influences can be prevented through good preconception and antenatal care.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics II – Maternal, Prenatal and Genetic Influences on Development of Defects and Diseases
question: Explain neural tube defects and the role of folic acid in their prevention.
answer_html:
Definition Neural tube defects (NTDs) are serious birth defects of the brain and spinal cord caused by failure of the neural tube to close during the fourth week after conception (by day 28) – often before a woman knows she is pregnant. India has one of the highest burdens of NTDs in the world.

1. Types A. Open NTDs

  • Anencephaly – absence of most of the brain and skull vault; incompatible with life.
  • Spina bifida aperta:
    • Meningocele – sac containing meninges and CSF; usually no paralysis.
    • Myelomeningocele – sac containing meninges, spinal cord and nerve roots (most common and severe, usually lumbosacral) → paralysis of legs, loss of bladder and bowel control, often with hydrocephalus (Arnold–Chiari II malformation).
    • Rachischisis/myeloschisis – open spinal cord.
  • Encephalocele – brain tissue protruding through a skull defect (usually occipital).

B. Closed NTD

  • Spina bifida occulta – defect of vertebral arches covered by skin; may show a tuft of hair, dimple, lipoma or birthmark over the lower back; usually symptomless.

2. Risk factors

  • Folic acid deficiency (most important preventable cause).
  • Previous NTD-affected pregnancy (recurrence risk 2–5%), family history.
  • Maternal diabetes, obesity, high fever in early pregnancy.
  • Antiepileptic drugs (valproate, carbamazepine), methotrexate.
  • Genetic factors (e.g. MTHFR variants), poor socio-economic status.

3. Role of folic acid in prevention

  • Folic acid is needed for DNA synthesis and cell division in the rapidly growing neural tube.
  • Periconceptional supplementation prevents a large proportion (50–70%) of NTDs:
    • 400 µg (0.4 mg) daily for all women planning pregnancy, from at least one month before conception until 12 weeks.
    • 4–5 mg daily for women with a previous NTD, on antiepileptics, with diabetes or obesity.
  • Public health measures in India: weekly IFA supplementation for adolescent girls, IFA under Anaemia Mukt Bharat, and fortification of rice and wheat flour with folic acid distributed through public programmes.
  • Dietary sources: green leafy vegetables, pulses, citrus fruits, liver.

4. Detection

  • Raised maternal serum AFP (16–18 weeks); ultrasound anomaly scan ("lemon" and "banana" signs, absent skull vault in anencephaly); amniotic fluid AFP and acetylcholinesterase.

5. Nursing care of a newborn with myelomeningocele

  • Keep the baby prone or side-lying; cover the sac with a sterile, warm, saline-moistened non-adherent dressing and protect it from rupture and infection; latex precautions.
  • Measure head circumference daily (hydrocephalus – shunt surgery), assess leg movement, bladder and bowel function.
  • Prepare for early surgical closure; support parents; long-term rehabilitation, clean intermittent catheterisation and physiotherapy.

Conclusion NTDs result from failure of neural tube closure by day 28 of development and range from anencephaly to spina bifida occulta. Periconceptional folic acid and food fortification can prevent most of them, making folic acid one of the most effective tools in preventive nursing.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics II – Maternal, Prenatal and Genetic Influences on Development of Defects and Diseases
question: Explain the genetic causes of infertility and spontaneous abortion.
answer_html:
Introduction Infertility affects about 10–15% of couples, and spontaneous abortion (miscarriage) ends about 10–15% of recognised pregnancies. Genetic factors play an important role in both, and identifying them helps in counselling and choosing treatment.

A. Genetic causes of spontaneous abortion

  1. Chromosomal abnormalities in the embryo – found in about 50–60% of first-trimester miscarriages:
    • Autosomal trisomies (most common – especially trisomy 16, also 21, 22, 15).
    • Monosomy X (45,X) – the commonest single abnormality.
    • Triploidy and tetraploidy.
    • Mostly sporadic (non-disjunction), more common with advanced maternal age; recurrence risk is usually low.
  2. Recurrent pregnancy loss (two or three or more consecutive miscarriages):
    • Balanced chromosomal translocations in one parent (found in about 2–5% of such couples) – produce unbalanced embryos; karyotyping of both partners is advised.
    • Single-gene disorders lethal to the embryo (rare).
  3. Non-genetic causes (uterine abnormalities, antiphospholipid syndrome, uncontrolled diabetes, thyroid disease, infections) must also be excluded.

B. Genetic causes of female infertility

  • Turner syndrome (45,X and mosaics) – streak ovaries, primary amenorrhoea, short stature.
  • Fragile X premutation – premature ovarian insufficiency.
  • Androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY) – female appearance, absent uterus, primary amenorrhoea.
  • Kallmann syndrome – hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with loss of smell.
  • Congenital adrenal hyperplasia, galactosaemia; PCOS (polygenic tendency).

C. Genetic causes of male infertility

  • Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) – most common genetic cause; small firm testes, azoospermia, gynaecomastia, tall stature.
  • Y-chromosome microdeletions (AZF regions) – azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia; can be passed to sons by ICSI.
  • CFTR (cystic fibrosis gene) mutations – congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (obstructive azoospermia).
  • Robertsonian and reciprocal translocations, Kallmann syndrome, primary ciliary dyskinesia (immotile sperm), 46,XX male.
  • Genetic testing (karyotype, Y-microdeletion) is advised when the sperm count is very low (e.g. below 5 million/mL) or absent.

D. Implications

  • Genetic counselling before IVF/ICSI; pre-implantation genetic testing; donor gametes; testing products of conception after miscarriage.
  • Counselling should stress that men contribute to infertility as often as women – correcting the unfair blame often placed on women in India.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses provide emotional support after miscarriage, encourage evaluation of both partners, and explain that most single miscarriages are due to chance chromosomal errors and not to the mother's activities.

Conclusion Chromosomal errors cause most early miscarriages, and balanced parental translocations explain some recurrent losses. Turner and Klinefelter syndromes, Y-microdeletions, CFTR mutations and other genetic conditions cause infertility, making genetic evaluation and counselling an important part of reproductive care.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics II – Maternal, Prenatal and Genetic Influences on Development of Defects and Diseases
question: Name the infections that can be dangerous during pregnancy.
answer_html:
Infections dangerous during pregnancy (can harm the foetus) – remembered as TORCH and others:

  1. T – Toxoplasmosis – hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, intracranial calcification.
  2. O – Others: syphilis (congenital syphilis, stillbirth), varicella (limb and skin defects), parvovirus B19 (hydrops), HIV, hepatitis B, Zika virus (microcephaly), Listeria, malaria.
  3. R – Rubella – congenital rubella syndrome (cataract, deafness, heart defects).
  4. C – Cytomegalovirus – deafness, microcephaly (most common congenital infection).
  5. H – Herpes simplex – severe neonatal infection.

Effects include miscarriage, stillbirth, birth defects, growth restriction and preterm birth; prevention – rubella (MR) vaccination before pregnancy, safe food and hygiene, antenatal screening (syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B) and treatment.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics II – Maternal, Prenatal and Genetic Influences on Development of Defects and Diseases
question: Write two causes of congenital abnormalities.
answer_html:
Causes of congenital abnormalities

  1. Genetic causes – chromosomal abnormalities (e.g. Down syndrome – trisomy 21) and single-gene defects (e.g. achondroplasia, cystic fibrosis).
  2. Environmental causes (teratogens) – drugs (thalidomide, valproate, isotretinoin), maternal infections (rubella, CMV, toxoplasmosis), radiation, alcohol, maternal diabetes and folic acid deficiency.

Others: multifactorial causes (genes plus environment – cleft lip and palate, neural tube defects, congenital heart disease); in about half the cases the cause remains unknown.

Prevention: periconceptional folic acid, rubella vaccination, avoiding teratogenic drugs, alcohol and tobacco, good control of maternal diabetes, and genetic counselling for high-risk couples.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics II – Maternal, Prenatal and Genetic Influences on Development of Defects and Diseases
question: Explain consanguinity and atopy.
answer_html:
Consanguinity is marriage or mating between blood relatives (second cousins or closer), such as first-cousin or uncle–niece marriages, which are customary in some communities of South India and elsewhere. Because relatives share genes from a common ancestor, both partners are more likely to carry the same harmful recessive gene, so their children have a higher risk of autosomal recessive disorders (thalassaemia, metabolic disorders) and birth defects. Genetic counselling and carrier screening are advised.

Atopy is an inherited tendency to produce IgE antibodies against common environmental allergens, leading to allergic diseases – asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic eczema and food allergy. Children of atopic parents have a higher risk; environmental factors (smoking, pollution) increase it.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics II – Maternal, Prenatal and Genetic Influences on Development of Defects and Diseases
question: What is a teratogen? Give examples.
answer_html:
A teratogen is any agent that causes structural or functional abnormalities in the developing embryo or foetus when the mother is exposed during pregnancy. The period of organogenesis (3–8 weeks after conception) is the most sensitive.

Examples

  1. Drugs – thalidomide (limb defects), isotretinoin, valproate (neural tube defects), warfarin, ACE inhibitors, tetracycline, methotrexate.
  2. Infections – rubella, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, syphilis, Zika virus.
  3. Physical agents – ionising radiation, high maternal fever.
  4. Chemicals and substances – alcohol, tobacco, lead, mercury.
  5. Maternal conditions – uncontrolled diabetes, phenylketonuria.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics III – Genetic Testing in the Neonates and Children
question: Explain newborn screening – conditions screened, method and the nurse's role.
answer_html:
Definition Newborn screening (NBS) is the testing of all newborn babies soon after birth to detect serious but treatable conditions before symptoms appear, so that early treatment can prevent death, intellectual disability and lifelong handicap. It is a key part of child-health programmes such as Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK).

1. Criteria for including a condition in screening

  • It is an important health problem; early treatment is effective; a simple, reliable test exists; benefits outweigh costs; facilities for confirmation and treatment are available.

2. Conditions commonly screened | Condition | Test | Why important | |---|---|---| | Congenital hypothyroidism (commonest; more frequent in India than in the West) | TSH on dried blood spot | Thyroxine started within the first 2 weeks prevents intellectual disability | | Congenital adrenal hyperplasia | 17-hydroxyprogesterone | Prevents salt-wasting crisis and death; helps gender assignment in ambiguous genitalia | | G6PD deficiency | Enzyme assay/fluorescent spot test | Prevents severe neonatal jaundice and drug-induced haemolysis | | Phenylketonuria (PKU) | Phenylalanine | Low-phenylalanine diet prevents brain damage | | Galactosaemia | Galactose/GALT enzyme | Galactose-free milk prevents liver failure, cataract, sepsis | | Biotinidase deficiency | Enzyme | Biotin supplements prevent seizures, deafness | | Sickle cell disease, thalassaemia | HPLC/electrophoresis (in high-prevalence areas) | Early penicillin prophylaxis, vaccines, counselling | | Hearing loss | Otoacoustic emissions (OAE), BERA | Early hearing aids/cochlear implant → normal speech | | Critical congenital heart disease | Pulse oximetry after 24 hours | Early cardiac referral | | Eye problems | Red reflex test; ROP screening in preterm babies | Prevents blindness | - Expanded screening by tandem mass spectrometry detects dozens of inborn errors from one blood spot (available in many private and some state programmes).

3. Method – heel-prick dried blood spot

  1. Collect after 24–48 hours of birth (ideally 48–72 hours), after feeds have started, and before discharge; repeat if taken earlier than 24 hours.
  2. Explain to parents and obtain consent; warm the heel, clean with alcohol and allow to dry.
  3. Prick the medial or lateral plantar surface of the heel (never the centre or the back).
  4. Wipe away the first drop; let large drops fall on the filter paper to fill each circle completely from one side; do not squeeze ("milk") the heel or touch the circles.
  5. Dry the card horizontally at room temperature for 3–4 hours away from sunlight and heat; do not stack wet cards.
  6. Fill details correctly (name, date and time of birth and collection, feeding, prematurity, transfusion, antibiotics) and dispatch within 24–48 hours.

4. Nurse's role

  • Educate parents about the purpose and importance of screening and follow-up.
  • Ensure correct sample collection, labelling and dispatch; maintain registers.
  • Trace and recall babies with positive results quickly for confirmatory tests; reassure that a positive screen is not a final diagnosis.
  • Support early treatment (e.g. daily thyroxine), diet counselling, and referral to District Early Intervention Centres; genetic counselling for families.

Conclusion Newborn screening by heel-prick blood spot, hearing tests and pulse oximetry detects conditions like congenital hypothyroidism, CAH, G6PD deficiency and PKU before damage occurs. Good sample collection and quick follow-up by nurses make the programme successful.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics III – Genetic Testing in the Neonates and Children
question: Explain the screening of newborns for congenital abnormalities at birth.
answer_html:
Introduction About 3–6% of babies are born with a congenital anomaly. Many can be detected by a careful head-to-toe examination at birth and treated early – often with excellent results (e.g. cleft lip repair, CTEV correction). Under RBSK, every newborn is screened for "4 Ds" – Defects at birth, Deficiencies, Diseases and Developmental delays including disabilities – at delivery points and during home visits.

1. When and who

  • Within the first 24 hours and again before discharge, by doctors, staff nurses and ANMs at the delivery point; later by mobile health teams at anganwadis and schools.

2. Systematic newborn examination | Area | What to look for | |---|---| | General | Weight, length, head circumference, colour (cyanosis, jaundice), cry, dysmorphic features | | Head | Microcephaly, hydrocephalus, fontanelles, encephalocele, cephalhaematoma | | Eyes | Red reflex (absent in congenital cataract, retinoblastoma), coloboma, small eyes | | Ears | Low-set ears, ear tags, pits, absent canal | | Mouth | Cleft lip and cleft palate (feel the palate), tongue-tie, natal teeth | | Neck and chest | Webbing, swellings; breathing pattern | | Heart | Murmurs, femoral pulses, pulse oximetry for critical heart disease | | Abdomen | Masses, omphalocele, gastroschisis, single umbilical artery | | Genitalia | Hypospadias, undescended testes, ambiguous genitalia | | Anus | Imperforate anus – check patency and passage of meconium within 24 hours | | Spine | Neural tube defects, sacral dimple, tuft of hair, swelling | | Limbs | Club foot (CTEV), polydactyly, syndactyly, limb reduction; hip – Ortolani and Barlow tests for developmental dysplasia | | Neurological | Tone, Moro, sucking and grasp reflexes | | Others | Down syndrome features, oesophageal atresia (frothing; pass a feeding tube if suspected) |

3. Common birth defects in India

  • Congenital heart disease, neural tube defects, cleft lip/palate, club foot, Down syndrome, hypospadias, congenital cataract, congenital deafness, developmental dysplasia of the hip.

4. Action after detection

  • Explain findings sensitively to parents; avoid blame.
  • Immediate care – e.g. cover NTD sac, keep NPO and refer in oesophageal atresia or imperforate anus, special feeding for cleft palate.
  • Referral to the District Early Intervention Centre (DEIC) and higher centres for confirmation and free treatment under RBSK.
  • Record in registers and on the MCP card; genetic counselling for recurrence risk.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • The staff nurse in the labour room is often the first to notice an anomaly; a systematic examination prevents missed diagnoses such as imperforate anus or cleft palate that can lead to serious complications.

Conclusion A systematic head-to-toe examination at birth detects most visible congenital anomalies. Early detection, sensitive communication, immediate care and referral through RBSK and DEICs give these babies the best chance of normal life.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics III – Genetic Testing in the Neonates and Children
question: What is developmental delay? Explain its causes, red flags, evaluation and management.
answer_html:
Definition Developmental delay is a significant lag in attaining developmental milestones compared with children of the same age, in one or more domains – gross motor, fine motor, speech and language, social–emotional and cognitive. When two or more domains are delayed in a child below 5 years, it is called global developmental delay (GDD). Early identification allows early intervention during the period of maximum brain plasticity.

1. Causes A. Genetic

  • Chromosomal – Down syndrome, microdeletions (22q11.2).
  • Single-gene – fragile X syndrome (most common inherited cause of intellectual disability), Rett syndrome, neurocutaneous syndromes.
  • Metabolic and endocrine – PKU, other inborn errors, congenital hypothyroidism.

B. Prenatal (environmental)

  • TORCH infections, alcohol, teratogenic drugs, maternal malnutrition, iodine deficiency.

C. Perinatal

  • Prematurity and low birth weight, birth asphyxia (hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy), severe neonatal jaundice (kernicterus), neonatal hypoglycaemia and sepsis.

D. Postnatal

  • Meningitis, encephalitis, head injury, severe malnutrition, lead poisoning, psychosocial deprivation and lack of stimulation.
  • In many children the cause remains unknown.

2. Red flags (refer for evaluation)

  • No social smile by 2–3 months; no head control by 4 months.
  • Not sitting without support by 9 months; not walking by 18 months.
  • No words by 16 months; no two-word phrases by 24 months; no response to name by 12 months (autism).
  • Persistent primitive reflexes, very floppy or stiff limbs.
  • Loss of previously acquired skills (regression) at any age – urgent referral.

3. Evaluation

  • Detailed history (pregnancy, birth, family history, consanguinity), growth and head circumference, examination for dysmorphic features, neurological examination.
  • Developmental screening tools – Trivandrum Developmental Screening Chart (TDSC) (Indian, quick), Denver Developmental Screening Test (DDST-II), Language Evaluation Scale Trivandrum (LEST), M-CHAT for autism; detailed assessment by DASII.
  • Hearing and vision tests, thyroid function, metabolic screening.
  • Genetic tests – chromosomal microarray (first-line), karyotype (Down syndrome), fragile X testing; MRI brain and EEG when indicated.

4. Management

  • Early intervention – physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, special education, behaviour therapy; parent training in home stimulation.
  • Treat the cause where possible (thyroxine, diet in PKU, nutrition rehabilitation).
  • District Early Intervention Centres (DEIC) under RBSK provide free multidisciplinary care; disability certification and benefits under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016.
  • Genetic counselling about recurrence risk.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses monitor milestones at every immunisation and well-baby visit using the MCP card, identify red flags early, counsel parents on play and stimulation, and support families emotionally.

Conclusion Developmental delay has genetic, prenatal, perinatal and postnatal causes. Early recognition through red flags and screening tools, followed by genetic evaluation and early intervention, greatly improves the child's outcome.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics III – Genetic Testing in the Neonates and Children
question: What is dysmorphism?
answer_html:
Dysmorphism means the presence of abnormal physical features (abnormal morphology), especially of the face, hands and feet, which result from abnormal development before birth. The study of such features to identify syndromes is called dysmorphology.

  • Examples of dysmorphic features: wide-set eyes (hypertelorism), upward-slanting eyes with epicanthic folds, low-set or malformed ears, flat nasal bridge, smooth philtrum and thin upper lip, single palmar crease, incurved little finger, sandal gap.
  • Significance: three or more minor anomalies suggest an underlying major anomaly or genetic syndrome (e.g. Down syndrome, Edwards syndrome, foetal alcohol syndrome); they guide genetic testing and counselling.
  • The nurse should record and report such features noticed during newborn examination.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics III – Genetic Testing in the Neonates and Children
question: Write a short note on fragile X syndrome.
answer_html:
Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and a common genetic cause of autism.

  • Genetics: X-linked; due to expansion of CGG trinucleotide repeats in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome (more than 200 repeats = full mutation; 55–200 = premutation); repeats expand when passed through mothers (anticipation).
  • Features (mainly boys): intellectual disability, autism-like behaviour, hyperactivity, poor eye contact; long face, large protruding ears, prominent jaw, hyperextensible joints, large testes (macro-orchidism) after puberty. Girls are usually milder.
  • Premutation carriers: premature ovarian insufficiency in women; tremor–ataxia syndrome in older men.
  • Diagnosis: DNA testing (PCR, Southern blot); management – special education, speech and behaviour therapy, and genetic counselling of the family.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics IV – Genetic Conditions of Adolescents and Adults
question: Explain cancer genetics with special reference to familial (hereditary) cancer syndromes.
answer_html:
Introduction Cancer is a genetic disease of cells – it results from mutations in oncogenes, tumour-suppressor genes and DNA-repair genes. Most cancers are sporadic, arising from mutations acquired during life; only about 5–10% are hereditary, due to an inherited (germline) mutation that greatly increases cancer risk in a family.

1. Sporadic versus familial cancer | Feature | Sporadic cancer | Familial/hereditary cancer | |---|---|---| | Cause | Acquired (somatic) mutations – age, tobacco, alcohol, infections, radiation, diet | Inherited germline mutation + additional acquired mutations | | Frequency | 90–95% | 5–10% | | Age at onset | Usually older | Younger (often below 50 years) | | Family history | Usually absent | Several relatives, across generations | | Tumours | Usually single | Bilateral or multiple primary cancers |

Knudson's "two-hit" hypothesis (retinoblastoma): both copies of a tumour-suppressor gene must be inactivated; in hereditary cases the first hit is inherited, so cancer develops earlier and often bilaterally.

2. Features suggesting hereditary cancer

  • Cancer at an unusually young age; two or more close relatives on the same side with related cancers; bilateral breast cancer; breast and ovarian cancer in one family; colon and endometrial cancer together; male breast cancer; rare tumours.

3. Important familial cancer syndromes | Syndrome | Gene | Main cancers | |---|---|---| | Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer | BRCA1, BRCA2 (AD) | Breast (lifetime risk up to 45–70%), ovary, prostate, pancreas, male breast | | Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) | Mismatch-repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) (AD) | Colorectal, endometrial, ovary, stomach, urinary tract | | Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) | APC (AD) | Hundreds to thousands of colonic polyps from teenage years; nearly 100% colorectal cancer if untreated | | Li–Fraumeni syndrome | TP53 | Sarcomas, breast, brain tumours, leukaemia, adrenal cancer | | Hereditary retinoblastoma | RB1 | Bilateral retinoblastoma, later osteosarcoma | | Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 | RET | Medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma | | Von Hippel–Lindau | VHL | Renal cell carcinoma, haemangioblastomas |

4. Management of families

  1. Genetic counselling and testing – usually first in an affected person, then cascade testing of relatives.
  2. Intensive screening – e.g. yearly mammography/breast MRI from 25–30 years in BRCA carriers; colonoscopy every 1–2 years from 20–25 years in Lynch syndrome.
  3. Risk-reducing surgery – mastectomy, removal of ovaries and tubes after childbearing (BRCA), colectomy (FAP), prophylactic thyroidectomy (RET carriers).
  4. Chemoprevention (tamoxifen) and targeted treatment (PARP inhibitors in BRCA-related cancers).
  5. Healthy lifestyle – avoid tobacco and alcohol, maintain weight.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses collect family histories, identify high-risk families, explain screening schedules, and support patients emotionally through testing and risk-reducing decisions.

Conclusion Most cancers are sporadic, but 5–10% are due to inherited mutations such as BRCA1/2, mismatch-repair genes, APC and TP53. Recognising familial patterns allows genetic testing, intensive screening and preventive measures that save lives.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics IV – Genetic Conditions of Adolescents and Adults
question: Write a note on inborn errors of metabolism.
answer_html:
Definition Inborn errors of metabolism (IEM) – a term introduced by Sir Archibald Garrod (1908) – are inherited disorders in which deficiency of a specific enzyme or transport protein blocks a metabolic pathway. This causes accumulation of toxic substances before the block and/or deficiency of essential products after it. Most are autosomal recessive and are more common in consanguineous families.

1. Classification with examples A. Disorders of amino acid metabolism

  • Phenylketonuria (PKU) – phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency; musty/mousy odour, fair skin, intellectual disability, seizures; treated with low-phenylalanine diet.
  • Alkaptonuria – urine turns black on standing, dark pigmentation of cartilage (ochronosis), arthritis.
  • Albinism (tyrosinase deficiency), maple syrup urine disease (sweet odour, neonatal encephalopathy), homocystinuria (lens dislocation, thrombosis, tall stature).

B. Disorders of carbohydrate metabolism

  • Galactosaemia – vomiting, jaundice, liver enlargement, cataract, E. coli sepsis after starting milk; galactose-free (lactose-free) diet.
  • Glycogen storage diseases (e.g. von Gierke disease – hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly; Pompe disease – cardiomyopathy), hereditary fructose intolerance.

C. Lysosomal storage disorders

  • Gaucher disease (hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain), Niemann–Pick disease, Tay–Sachs disease (cherry-red spot, neurodegeneration), Fabry disease, mucopolysaccharidoses (Hurler, Hunter – coarse facial features, organomegaly).

D. Other groups

  • Urea cycle disorders (hyperammonaemia), organic acidaemias (methylmalonic, propionic acidaemia), fatty-acid oxidation defects, Wilson's disease (copper), porphyrias, Lesch–Nyhan syndrome.

2. Clinical clues

  • A baby who is well at birth and becomes ill after feeds begin – poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, seizures, coma (often mistaken for sepsis).
  • Unusual body or urine odour, metabolic acidosis, hypoglycaemia, high ammonia, jaundice, liver enlargement, cataract.
  • Later – developmental delay or regression, organomegaly, coarse features; history of unexplained sibling deaths or consanguinity.

3. Diagnosis

  • Newborn screening (tandem mass spectrometry); blood ammonia, lactate, gases, glucose; urine organic acids, plasma amino acids; enzyme assays; DNA testing; prenatal diagnosis in future pregnancies.

4. Treatment

  • Dietary restriction of the offending substance (phenylalanine, galactose, protein) with special formulas.
  • Supplementation of deficient products or cofactors (biotin, vitamin B12).
  • Removal of toxic metabolites (dialysis, sodium benzoate in hyperammonaemia).
  • Enzyme replacement therapy (Gaucher, Fabry, Pompe, MPS) – very costly; financial support is available under India's National Policy for Rare Diseases (2021) at Centres of Excellence.
  • Liver or bone-marrow transplantation; gene therapy (emerging).

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses collect newborn screening samples, recognise the "sick neonate after feeds", support strict lifelong diets, teach parents emergency plans during illness, and refer for genetic counselling.

Conclusion Inborn errors of metabolism are mostly autosomal recessive enzyme defects affecting amino acid, carbohydrate, lipid and other pathways. Early detection by newborn screening and prompt dietary or enzyme treatment can prevent brain damage and death.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics IV – Genetic Conditions of Adolescents and Adults
question: Explain thalassaemia – its genetic basis, types, diagnosis and prevention.
answer_html:
Definition Thalassaemias are inherited (autosomal recessive) disorders of haemoglobin in which there is reduced or absent synthesis of one type of globin chain (α or β). The imbalance of chains causes ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis, producing microcytic hypochromic anaemia. β-thalassaemia is a major public health problem in India, with many lakh carriers and thousands of children born with thalassaemia major every year.

1. Genetic basis

  • β-thalassaemia – mutations in the β-globin gene (HBB) on chromosome 11 (mostly point and splice-site mutations); β⁰ (no β-chain) or β⁺ (reduced).
  • α-thalassaemia – mostly deletions of α-globin genes on chromosome 16 (four genes): one deleted – silent carrier; two – trait; three – HbH disease; four – Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis (lethal).
  • Inheritance: when both parents are carriers (thalassaemia minor), each pregnancy has a 25% chance of thalassaemia major, 50% of minor and 25% of normal child.
  • Higher carrier frequency in certain communities (e.g. Sindhi, Punjabi, Gujarati, Bengali and some tribal groups).

2. Types of β-thalassaemia | Type | Genotype | Features | |---|---|---| | Thalassaemia minor (trait) | One abnormal gene | Usually no or mild anaemia, low MCV; often mistaken for iron deficiency | | Thalassaemia intermedia | Milder mutations | Moderate anaemia; occasional transfusions | | Thalassaemia major (Cooley's anaemia) | Two abnormal genes | Severe anaemia from 6–24 months of age, hepatosplenomegaly, growth failure, "thalassaemic facies" (frontal bossing, prominent maxilla), "hair-on-end" skull X-ray; lifelong transfusions needed | - HbE-β-thalassaemia is common in eastern India.

3. Diagnosis

  • CBC – low Hb, low MCV (below 80 fL) and MCH, relatively high RBC count; Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) below 13 suggests thalassaemia trait.
  • Peripheral smear – microcytic hypochromic cells, target cells, nucleated RBCs.
  • HPLC/Hb electrophoresis – HbA2 above 3.5% in β-thalassaemia trait; very high HbF in thalassaemia major.
  • DNA analysis – mutation identification (needed for prenatal diagnosis).

4. Treatment of thalassaemia major

  • Regular blood transfusions every 2–4 weeks to keep pre-transfusion Hb around 9.5–10.5 g/dL.
  • Iron chelation – desferrioxamine (subcutaneous infusion), deferasirox or deferiprone (oral) – to prevent iron overload of heart, liver and endocrine glands.
  • Folic acid, vaccinations, splenectomy in hypersplenism.
  • Haematopoietic stem cell (bone-marrow) transplantation – the only established cure; gene therapy is emerging.

5. Prevention

  1. Carrier screening – premarital, school/college and antenatal screening (CBC, HPLC); partner testing if the woman is a carrier.
  2. Genetic counselling of carrier couples.
  3. Prenatal diagnosis by chorionic villus sampling at 10–13 weeks with DNA analysis, and termination if the foetus is affected, according to the couple's choice.
  4. Public awareness and community programmes; national guidelines on haemoglobinopathies support screening and free treatment.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses manage safe transfusions and chelation, monitor growth and iron overload, educate families, and promote carrier screening and counselling in the community.

Conclusion Thalassaemia is an autosomal recessive disorder of globin-chain synthesis that ranges from silent trait to transfusion-dependent major disease. Carrier screening, genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis can prevent most new cases, while transfusion and chelation keep affected children alive and well.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics IV – Genetic Conditions of Adolescents and Adults
question: Explain the genetic aspects of mental illness.
answer_html:
Introduction Most mental illnesses run in families, but they are not caused by a single gene. They are multifactorial disorders – many genes, each with a small effect (polygenic inheritance), interacting with environmental factors such as stress, trauma, substance use, infections and birth complications. Understanding this helps families accept illness without blame or fatalism.

1. Evidence for genetic influence

  • Family studies – higher risk in relatives of affected persons.
  • Twin studies – higher concordance in identical (monozygotic) than in non-identical twins.
  • Adoption studies – risk follows biological rather than adoptive parents.
  • Genome studies – many risk variants identified, each of small effect; a few rare variants of large effect.

2. Heritability and risk in common disorders | Disorder | Approximate heritability | Risk to relatives | |---|---|---| | Schizophrenia | About 80% | General population ~1%; one parent affected ~10–13%; both parents ~40%; identical twin ~40–50% | | Bipolar disorder | About 70–85% | First-degree relative ~5–10%; identical twin ~40–70% | | Autism spectrum disorder | About 80% | Sibling recurrence ~10–20% | | ADHD | About 70–80% | Increased in siblings and parents | | Major depression | About 35–40% | Two- to three-fold increase in first-degree relatives | | Alcohol dependence | About 50% | Higher in children of dependent parents | | OCD | About 40–50% | Increased in first-degree relatives |

3. Specific genetic syndromes with psychiatric features

  • 22q11.2 deletion syndrome – about a quarter develop schizophrenia-like psychosis.
  • Fragile X syndrome – autism, intellectual disability, anxiety.
  • Huntington's disease – depression, irritability, psychosis before chorea.
  • Down syndrome – early-onset Alzheimer's disease.
  • Alzheimer's disease – early-onset familial forms (APP, presenilin genes, autosomal dominant); APOE ε4 increases the risk of late-onset disease.

4. Gene–environment interaction

  • Genetic vulnerability + stressful life events, childhood abuse, cannabis use, urban stress, prenatal infections and obstetric complications → illness.
  • Epigenetic changes (chemical changes in gene expression) link environment and genes.
  • This explains why many people with a family history never develop illness, and why environmental prevention matters.

5. Pharmacogenomics in psychiatry

  • Variations in CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 enzymes affect blood levels of antidepressants and antipsychotics; HLA-B*1502 predicts carbamazepine-induced Stevens–Johnson syndrome in Asians.

6. Implications for practice

  • No routine genetic test diagnoses common mental illnesses; counselling uses empirical (observed) risk figures.
  • Families should be told that mental illness is not a curse, punishment or the parents' fault; risk is increased but not certain.
  • Early identification of at-risk children, avoidance of substance use, stress management and good perinatal care help prevention.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Psychiatric nurses take family histories, provide psychoeducation, reduce stigma, support marriage and pregnancy counselling, and promote early help-seeking (e.g. Tele-MANAS 14416), respecting rights under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017.

Conclusion Mental illnesses such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and autism have strong but polygenic genetic influences that interact with environmental stresses. This understanding guides counselling, prevention, stigma reduction and personalised treatment.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics IV – Genetic Conditions of Adolescents and Adults
question: Define sporadic cancer.
answer_html:
Sporadic cancer is cancer that occurs by chance in a person who has not inherited a cancer-predisposing gene mutation. It results from somatic mutations acquired during life in body cells, caused by ageing, tobacco, alcohol, infections (HPV, hepatitis B), radiation, diet and other environmental factors.

  • Most cancers (about 90–95%) are sporadic.
  • Features: later age of onset, usually a single tumour, no strong family history.
  • Examples: most lung cancers (smoking), oral cancers (tobacco chewing – very common in India), cervical cancer (HPV).
  • In contrast, hereditary (familial) cancer results from an inherited germline mutation (e.g. BRCA1/2).

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics IV – Genetic Conditions of Adolescents and Adults
question: Write a short note on haemochromatosis.
answer_html:
Haemochromatosis is a condition of excessive iron deposition in body tissues leading to organ damage.

  • Hereditary (primary) haemochromatosis – autosomal recessive, most often due to mutation of the HFE gene (C282Y) on chromosome 6 → increased intestinal iron absorption; common in people of northern European origin, rare in Indians.
  • Secondary haemochromatosis – due to repeated blood transfusions (e.g. thalassaemia major) – much more common in India.
  • Effects: liver cirrhosis and liver cancer, diabetes with skin pigmentation ("bronze diabetes"), cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias, arthritis, hypogonadism.
  • Diagnosis: raised transferrin saturation and serum ferritin, HFE gene test, liver MRI.
  • Treatment: regular phlebotomy (venesection); iron chelation for transfusional overload; avoid iron and vitamin C supplements and alcohol; screen family members.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics IV – Genetic Conditions of Adolescents and Adults
question: Write a short note on Huntington's disease.
answer_html:
Huntington's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.

  • Genetics: expansion of CAG trinucleotide repeats in the HTT (huntingtin) gene on chromosome 4 (40 or more repeats cause disease); repeats may expand in successive generations (anticipation), especially through the father; each child of an affected parent has a 50% risk.
  • Onset: usually 30–50 years.
  • Triad: chorea (involuntary, jerky, dance-like movements), cognitive decline/dementia, and psychiatric symptoms (depression, irritability, psychosis, suicide risk).
  • Pathology: atrophy of the caudate nucleus.
  • Management: no cure; drugs for chorea (tetrabenazine) and depression, physiotherapy, nutrition, family support.
  • Predictive genetic testing raises ethical issues – done only with counselling, respecting the right not to know; not done in children for adult-onset disease.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics V – Services related to Genetics
question: Write a short note on genetic counselling and its issues.
answer_html:
Definition Genetic counselling is the process of helping individuals and families understand and adapt to the medical, psychological and family implications of genetic contributions to disease. It combines interpretation of family and medical history, education about inheritance, testing and prevention, and counselling to support informed choices.

1. Indications

  • Family history of a genetic disorder (thalassaemia, sickle cell disease, haemophilia, muscular dystrophy).
  • Previous child with a birth defect, intellectual disability or genetic disease.
  • Consanguineous couples; advanced maternal age (35 years or more).
  • Recurrent miscarriage, stillbirths, infertility.
  • Abnormal prenatal screening or ultrasound findings; exposure to teratogens.
  • Carriers identified by screening; adult-onset disorders (Huntington's disease, familial cancers).

2. Steps of genetic counselling

  1. Establish rapport in a private, comfortable setting; identify the couple's concerns.
  2. History – medical, obstetric and three-generation pedigree.
  3. Diagnosis – examination and investigations to confirm the exact disorder (essential for accurate advice).
  4. Risk assessment – calculation of recurrence risk (Mendelian or empirical).
  5. Communication – nature of the disease, inheritance, risk, prognosis, treatment and available options (testing, prenatal diagnosis, pre-implantation testing, donor gametes, adoption, contraception, or accepting the risk).
  6. Support decision-making – in a non-directive way.
  7. Psychological support – for grief, guilt, anxiety and family conflict.
  8. Follow-up – written summary, testing of relatives (cascade testing), referral to support groups and services.

3. Principles

  • Non-directive approach, voluntariness, informed consent, confidentiality, truthfulness, respect for culture and religion, equity.

4. Issues in genetic counselling

  • Non-directiveness in the Indian context – families often expect to be told what to do.
  • Confidentiality versus duty to warn relatives at risk; disclosure of unexpected findings (e.g. misattributed paternity).
  • Sex selection pressure – counsellors must never reveal foetal sex (PCPNDT Act).
  • Prenatal diagnosis and termination – moral, religious and disability-rights concerns.
  • Stigma and marriage discrimination of carriers and affected persons; social pressure in arranged marriages.
  • Consanguinity – cultural tradition versus genetic risk; must be discussed sensitively.
  • Testing children for adult-onset disorders – generally postponed until adulthood.
  • Shortage of trained genetic counsellors, cost and urban concentration of services; language and literacy barriers.
  • Privacy of genetic data and possible misuse by employers or insurers.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses identify families in need, draw pedigrees, explain tests, provide emotional support and follow-up, and link families to programmes such as the sickle cell elimination mission, thalassaemia support groups and rare-disease services.

Conclusion Genetic counselling helps families understand genetic risks and make informed, autonomous choices through accurate diagnosis, risk assessment, education and support. Cultural, ethical and legal issues – non-directiveness, confidentiality, sex selection, stigma and access – require sensitive handling.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics V – Services related to Genetics
question: Explain the significance of genetic testing.
answer_html:
Definition Genetic testing is the analysis of chromosomes, DNA, RNA, proteins or metabolites to detect inherited or acquired genetic changes for medical purposes. Rapid advances (PCR, next-generation sequencing) have made many tests available in India.

1. Types of genetic tests (by purpose)

  1. Diagnostic testing – confirms a suspected disorder (karyotype for Down syndrome; DNA test for Duchenne muscular dystrophy).
  2. Predictive (presymptomatic) testing – in healthy persons at risk of adult-onset disease (Huntington's disease, BRCA mutations).
  3. Carrier testing – detects healthy carriers of recessive or X-linked genes (thalassaemia, sickle cell, haemophilia carriers).
  4. Prenatal testing – CVS, amniocentesis, cell-free DNA screening.
  5. Pre-implantation genetic testing – of embryos in IVF.
  6. Newborn screening – hypothyroidism, PKU, G6PD deficiency.
  7. Pharmacogenetic testing – predicts drug response or toxicity (HLA-B*1502 before carbamazepine, TPMT before azathioprine, G6PD before primaquine).
  8. Tumour (somatic) testing – EGFR, HER2, BCR-ABL to choose targeted cancer therapy.
  9. Forensic and identity testing – DNA fingerprinting for paternity, crime and disaster-victim identification.

2. Methods

  • Cytogenetic – karyotyping, FISH.
  • Molecular – PCR and its variants, MLPA, DNA sequencing (Sanger, next-generation – gene panels, exome, genome), chromosomal microarray.
  • Biochemical – enzyme assays, HPLC for haemoglobin variants, tandem mass spectrometry.

3. Significance (uses)

  1. Early and accurate diagnosis – ends long diagnostic searches; guides prognosis.
  2. Treatment choice – targeted therapy (e.g. imatinib in CML), avoiding harmful drugs, early dietary treatment (PKU).
  3. Prevention and surveillance – intensive cancer screening or risk-reducing surgery in carriers.
  4. Reproductive decision-making – carrier couples can choose prenatal or pre-implantation diagnosis.
  5. Family benefit – identifies at-risk relatives through cascade testing; reassures those testing negative.
  6. Public health – carrier screening programmes (e.g. sickle cell disease in tribal districts) reduce disease burden.
  7. Research and personalised medicine.

4. Limitations and concerns

  • Not all mutations are detectable; variants of uncertain significance; incomplete penetrance – a positive result is not always disease.
  • Psychological impact, anxiety, family conflict; cost; risk of discrimination and stigma; privacy of genetic data; direct-to-consumer tests without counselling.
  • Hence pre-test and post-test counselling and informed consent are essential.

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses explain the purpose, benefits and limits of tests, obtain consent, collect samples correctly, maintain confidentiality, and support patients when results are given.

Conclusion Genetic testing – diagnostic, predictive, carrier, prenatal, newborn, pharmacogenetic and tumour testing – improves diagnosis, treatment, prevention and family planning. Its benefits are realised only when accompanied by counselling, consent and confidentiality.

subject: Pathology II and Genetics
unit_title: Genetics V – Services related to Genetics
question: Write a note on gene therapy.
tags: in vivo and ex vivo gene therapy
answer_html:
Definition Gene therapy is the treatment of disease by introducing, altering, replacing or silencing genetic material in a patient's cells, to correct a genetic defect or give cells a new therapeutic function.

1. Types
