  • Somatic cell gene therapy – changes body cells; not passed to children; permitted under regulation.
  • Germline gene therapy – changes eggs, sperm or embryos; inherited by future generations; prohibited in India and most countries.
  • In vivo – the gene is delivered directly into the body (e.g. into the eye, liver or muscle).
  • Ex vivo – the patient's cells (e.g. blood stem cells or T-cells) are removed, modified in the laboratory and returned.

2. Approaches

  1. Gene addition – adding a normal copy of a defective gene (e.g. ADA-SCID, haemophilia, spinal muscular atrophy).
  2. Gene silencing – blocking a harmful gene with antisense or RNA-interference drugs.
  3. Gene editing – correcting or disabling a gene using tools such as CRISPR-Cas9 (approved abroad for sickle cell disease and β-thalassaemia).
  4. Immune gene therapy – CAR-T cells, the patient's T-cells engineered to attack cancer (India developed and approved its own CAR-T therapy in 2023 for B-cell blood cancers).
  5. Suicide-gene and oncolytic-virus therapy for cancers.

3. Vectors (carriers of genes)

  • Viral vectors – adeno-associated virus (AAV) (safe, non-integrating), lentivirus/retrovirus (integrate into DNA – long-lasting, risk of insertional mutation), adenovirus.
  • Non-viral – lipid nanoparticles, liposomes, electroporation, naked DNA.

4. Milestones

  • 1990 – first approved human gene therapy (ADA-deficient severe combined immunodeficiency, USA).
  • Later – therapies for inherited retinal blindness, spinal muscular atrophy, haemophilia B, sickle cell disease and β-thalassaemia; gene therapy trials for haemophilia have begun in India.

5. Indications (current and future)

  • Single-gene disorders – SCID, haemophilia, thalassaemia, sickle cell disease, spinal muscular atrophy, Duchenne muscular dystrophy (trials), inherited retinal diseases.
  • Cancers – CAR-T therapy for leukaemia and lymphoma.
  • Infections (HIV – trials), heart and neurological diseases (trials).

6. Risks and limitations

  • Immune and inflammatory reactions, cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity (CAR-T), insertional mutagenesis (leukaemia), off-target gene editing.
  • Short-lived effects in some cases; very high cost; complex manufacturing; long-term follow-up needed.
  • Ethical concerns – germline editing, "designer babies", equity of access.
  • In India, research is regulated by the ICMR National Guidelines for Gene Therapy Product Development and Clinical Trials (2019).

Applied / Nursing importance

  • Nurses educate patients, support informed consent, administer therapies under protocols, monitor for infusion reactions and cytokine release syndrome, follow biosafety precautions and ensure long-term follow-up.

Conclusion Gene therapy treats disease at its genetic root by adding, silencing or editing genes, delivered mainly by viral vectors. It offers cures for some inherited disorders and cancers but faces challenges of safety, cost and ethics.

question: Explain the legal and ethical issues related to genetics and the role of the nurse in genetic services.
tags: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act
answer_html:
Introduction Genetic information is personal, predictive and shared by families. Its use raises special ethical and legal issues about consent, privacy, discrimination, reproductive choices and new technologies. Nurses, working closely with families, must understand these issues and their professional role.

A. Ethical issues

  1. Autonomy and informed consent – complex information, low literacy and family pressure can limit true consent; the right to know and the right not to know must be respected.
  2. Confidentiality versus duty to warn – genetic results also affect relatives; disclosure must be handled with the patient's consent and counselling.
  3. Genetic discrimination and stigma – in marriage, education, employment and insurance; labelling of carriers.
  4. Testing of children for adult-onset conditions – generally deferred until the child can decide.
  5. Prenatal diagnosis and selective termination – conflict between parental choice and disability rights; fear of eugenics.
  6. Sex selection – misuse of technology against girl children.
  7. Incidental findings in genome tests and direct-to-consumer testing without counselling.
  8. New technologies – gene editing, germline modification, embryo selection.
  9. Justice – unequal access to costly tests and treatments (enzyme replacement, gene therapy).
  10. Genetic data and biobanks – ownership, privacy and commercial use.

B. Legal framework in India

  • PCPNDT Act, 1994 (amended 2003) – prohibits sex selection and disclosure of foetal sex; regulates prenatal diagnostic facilities.
  • MTP (Amendment) Act, 2021 – allows termination beyond 24 weeks for substantial foetal abnormalities on the decision of a Medical Board.
  • ART (Regulation) Act, 2021 and Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021 – regulate pre-implantation genetic testing (only for genetic disease) and prohibit sex selection.
  • ICMR National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research (2017) – consent, genetic research, biobanking.
  • ICMR Gene Therapy Guidelines (2019) – germline therapy prohibited.
  • National Policy for Rare Diseases (2021) – financial support for treatment at Centres of Excellence.
  • Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 – includes intellectual disability and blood disorders (haemophilia, thalassaemia, sickle cell disease) among disabilities, ensuring rights and benefits.
  • Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 – consent and protection for processing personal data.

C. Role of the nurse in genetic services

  1. Identification – family history, pedigree, recognising red flags and at-risk families.
  2. Education – inheritance, tests, prevention (folic acid, avoidance of teratogens, carrier screening).
  3. Counselling support – pre-test and post-test support, emotional care, correcting blame.
  4. Sample collection and screening – newborn screening, antenatal carrier screening, community screening camps.
  5. Direct care – children and adults with genetic disorders (transfusions, chelation, developmental care).
  6. Coordination and referral – genetic clinics, DEICs, support groups, government schemes.
  7. Advocacy – rights of persons with genetic conditions, access to services, anti-stigma work.
  8. Ethical and legal practice – informed consent, confidentiality, never disclosing foetal sex, reporting violations.
  9. Research – protecting participants and their data.
  10. Continuing education in genomics.

Conclusion Genetics raises issues of consent, privacy, discrimination, reproductive choices and access, governed in India by the PCPNDT, MTP, ART and disability laws and ICMR guidelines. Nurses act as identifiers, educators, supporters, advocates and ethical guardians in genetic services.

question: What is a pedigree chart? Mention the standard symbols used.
answer_html:
A pedigree chart is a diagram of a family history using standard symbols, usually covering three or more generations, to show family relationships and the occurrence of a trait or disease. It helps to identify the pattern of inheritance, calculate risk and find relatives who need testing.

Standard symbols

  • Square – male; circle – female; diamond – sex unknown.
  • Shaded symbol – affected; half-shaded or dot in the centre – carrier.
  • Horizontal line between a square and a circle – marriage/mating; double line – consanguineous marriage.
  • Vertical line down to a horizontal sibship line – children.
  • Diagonal line through a symbol – deceased.
  • Arrow – proband (index case).
  • Generations are numbered with Roman numerals (I, II, III) and individuals with Arabic numerals.

question: What is pharmacogenomics? Give examples.
answer_html:
Pharmacogenomics is the study of how a person's genetic make-up affects his or her response to drugs – their effectiveness and their adverse effects. It is the basis of personalised ("precision") medicine – the right drug and dose for the right person.

Examples

  1. G6PD deficiency – haemolysis with primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides.
  2. HLA-B*1502 (common in South and South-East Asians) – high risk of Stevens–Johnson syndrome with carbamazepine and phenytoin.
  3. TPMT/NUDT15 variants – severe bone-marrow toxicity with azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine.
  4. CYP2C19 poor metabolisers – clopidogrel less effective; CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers – codeine toxicity.
  5. Slow acetylators – isoniazid neuropathy (prevented by pyridoxine).
